LIVER__Foundations of Metabolism:
Overview — Glycolysis
📷 Image placeholder — glycolysis pathway overview — glucose through 10 steps to 2 pyruvate, showing the 2-ATP investment phase, the 4-ATP + 2-NADH payoff phase, and the three irreversible control enzymes (hexokinase, PFK-1 [rate-limiting], pyruvate kinase)
Glycolysis is the first step in glucose metabolism — splitting glucose into pyruvate to release energy, in every cell, with or without oxygen.
The organising principle: glycolysis takes one glucose → two pyruvate, producing a small amount of ATP + NADH, in the cytoplasm — and crucially it can run anaerobically (no oxygen needed), which is why it's the emergency energy pathway. Its fate (aerobic → Krebs, or anaerobic → lactate) depends on oxygen.
Why it matters: underpins lactic acidosis, the Warburg effect in cancer, red cell metabolism, and how the body makes energy without oxygen (ischaemia, exercise) — cross-ref Krebs cycle + oxidative phosphorylation (the next subtabs), glucose homeostasis, lactic acidosis, red cell physiology.
The Essentials — the spine
Feature Glycolysis
LocationCytoplasm (not mitochondria — so no oxygen/mitochondria needed)
Input1 glucose (6 carbons)
Output2 pyruvate (3 carbons each) + 2 ATP (net) + 2 NADH
Oxygen needed?NO — runs aerobically or anaerobically

The Pathway in Concept — the logic, not every enzyme
Glucose is progressively broken down through 10 steps, conceptually in two halves:
Investment phase
  • 2 ATP are used to phosphorylate glucose (trapping it in the cell + priming it)
Payoff phase
  • The molecule splits and is processed → 4 ATP + 2 NADH produced
Net yield: 4 produced − 2 invested = 2 ATP net + 2 NADH + 2 pyruvate per glucose.
The point: glycolysis is energy-inexpensive but quick — it gives only 2 ATP (vs ~30+ from full aerobic metabolism), but it's fast and doesn't need oxygen.
The Key Regulated Enzymes — the control points
Three irreversible steps control the pathway:
Enzyme Role Regulation
Hexokinase/glucokinaseFirst step (traps glucose as glucose-6-phosphate)Glucokinase in liver (high capacity, glucose sensor)
Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1)The rate-limiting/committed stepActivated by AMP/ADP (low energy → speed up); inhibited by ATP + citrate (high energy → slow down)
Pyruvate kinaseLast step (makes pyruvate + ATP)Regulated by energy state
PFK-1 is the key control point: it's the rate-limiting, committed step → low energy (↑AMP) speeds glycolysis up; high energy (↑ATP, ↑citrate) slows it down → the cell makes ATP when it needs it.
Hormonal control: insulin stimulates glycolysis (fed state — use/store glucose); glucagon inhibits it (fasted state — preserve glucose) — cross-ref glucose homeostasis.
The Fate of Pyruvate — the oxygen-dependent fork (core concept)
What happens to pyruvate depends on oxygen availability:
Condition Fate of pyruvate Result
Aerobic (O₂ present)Pyruvate → acetyl-CoA → Krebs cycle → oxidative phosphorylationFull ATP yield (~30+ per glucose)
Anaerobic (no O₂)Pyruvate → lactate (via lactate dehydrogenase)Only 2 ATP, but glycolysis can keep running
Why anaerobic glycolysis matters (the key point): glycolysis needs NAD⁺ to keep going (it's consumed making NADH). Aerobically, the mitochondria regenerate NAD⁺. Anaerobically, converting pyruvate → lactate regenerates NAD⁺ → allowing glycolysis (and thus ATP production) to continue without oxygen.
The trade-off: anaerobic glycolysis lets cells make ATP without oxygen (emergency energy), but it's inefficient (2 ATP) and produces lactate → lactic acidosis if sustained.

Overview — Krebs Cycle (Citric Acid / TCA Cycle)
📷 Image placeholder — the Krebs (citric acid) cycle wheel — acetyl-CoA (2C) + oxaloacetate (4C) → citrate, cycling back to oxaloacetate while releasing 2 CO₂, 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂ and 1 GTP per turn
The Krebs cycle is the central hub of aerobic metabolism — it takes the products of carbohydrate, fat, and protein breakdown and extracts their energy as electron carriers (NADH, FADH₂) for the final ATP-generating step.
The organising principle: the cycle takes acetyl-CoA (the common product of glucose, fat, and protein breakdown) and oxidises it, capturing energy as NADH + FADH₂ (which feed oxidative phosphorylation) and releasing CO₂. It's a cycle (regenerates its starting molecule) and is strictly aerobic and mitochondrial.
Why it matters: it's the convergence point of all fuel metabolism, explains why metabolism needs oxygen, and the role of B vitamins/thiamine — cross-ref glycolysis (the input), oxidative phosphorylation (where NADH/FADH₂ go), fed/fasted state, fatty acid oxidation.
The Essentials — the spine
Feature Krebs cycle
LocationMitochondrial matrix (not cytoplasm — unlike glycolysis)
InputAcetyl-CoA (2 carbons)
Output per cycle3 NADH + 1 FADH₂ + 1 GTP (≈ATP) + 2 CO₂
Oxygen needed?Indirectly YES — needs oxidative phosphorylation to regenerate NAD⁺/FAD (so it stops without O₂)
PurposeExtract energy as NADH + FADH₂ (electron carriers) for the electron transport chain
Per glucose: glycolysis makes 2 pyruvate → 2 acetyl-CoA → 2 turns of the cycle → so double the per-cycle output.
The Link Reaction — pyruvate → acetyl-CoA
Before the cycle, pyruvate (from glycolysis) must become acetyl-CoA:
  • Pyruvate → acetyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH, by the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex
The thiamine point: PDH (and a Krebs enzyme) require thiamine (vitamin B1) as a cofactor → thiamine deficiency (alcoholism, malnutrition) → impaired pyruvate metabolism → lactate builds up + energy failure → Wernicke's encephalopathy / beriberi (why alcoholics get IV thiamine — Pabrinex).
PDH is a key irreversible commitment — once pyruvate → acetyl-CoA, it's committed to oxidation (can't go back to glucose).
The Cycle in Concept — the logic
Acetyl-CoA (2C) combines with oxaloacetate (4C) → citrate (6C) → progressively oxidised back to oxaloacetate, releasing:
  • 2 CO₂ (the carbons leave as carbon dioxide — exhaled)
  • 3 NADH + 1 FADH₂ (the energy, captured as electron carriers)
  • 1 GTP (≈ 1 ATP, direct)
The point: the cycle's real job is not to make ATP directly (only 1 GTP) — it's to harvest high-energy electrons as NADH + FADH₂, which are then "cashed in" for lots of ATP in oxidative phosphorylation (the next step).
It regenerates oxaloacetate at the end → so it's a continuous cycle.
Why It Needs Oxygen — the key dependency
The Krebs cycle has no direct oxygen step, but it stops without oxygen — because:
  • It consumes NAD⁺ and FAD (converting them to NADH/FADH₂)
  • These must be regenerated by oxidative phosphorylation (which needs O₂)
  • No O₂ → NADH/FADH₂ can't be reoxidised → NAD⁺/FAD run out → the cycle halts
This is why anaerobic tissue relies on glycolysis + lactate (cross-ref glycolysis): without O₂, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation stop, so glycolysis→lactate is the only ATP source.
The Cycle as a Metabolic Crossroads — the convergence point
All three macronutrients converge on the Krebs cycle as acetyl-CoA (or cycle intermediates):
Fuel Route into the cycle
CarbohydrateGlucose → glycolysis → pyruvate → acetyl-CoA
FatFatty acids → β-oxidation → acetyl-CoA (cross-ref)
ProteinAmino acids → various cycle intermediates (or acetyl-CoA)
The point: the Krebs cycle is the common final pathway for extracting energy from all fuels — they all funnel through acetyl-CoA → the cycle → NADH/FADH₂ → ATP.
Building blocks too: cycle intermediates are also used to make other molecules (for amino acids, glucose via gluconeogenesis, haem) → the cycle is both catabolic and a biosynthetic hub.
Regulation — energy-state controlled
  • Controlled by the cell's energy state: ↑ATP/NADH (high energy) → slows the cycle; ↑ADP/NAD⁺ (low energy) → speeds it up (like glycolysis)
  • The cycle is controlled by the cell's energy state, and PDH (the entry point) is also tightly regulated

Overview — Oxidative Phosphorylation & the Electron Transport Chain
📷 Image placeholder — the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane — complexes I–IV passing electrons from NADH/FADH₂ and pumping H⁺ to build the proton gradient, O₂ as the final electron acceptor at complex IV, and ATP synthase (complex V) making ATP as protons flow back
Oxidative phosphorylation is the final, major ATP-producing step — it cashes in the NADH and FADH₂ from glycolysis and the Krebs cycle to make the bulk of the cell's ATP, using oxygen.
The organising principle: NADH/FADH₂ donate electrons to the electron transport chain (ETC), which pumps protons to build a gradient; the protons then flow back through ATP synthase to make ATP — and oxygen is the final electron acceptor (which is why we breathe). This is where the great majority of the body's ATP is made.
Why it matters: explains why oxygen is essential for life, cyanide/CO poisoning, the link between breathing and energy, and metabolic poisons — cross-ref glycolysis + Krebs (the NADH/FADH₂ source), gas exchange (oxygen supply), cyanide poisoning, lactic acidosis.
The Essentials — the spine
Feature Oxidative phosphorylation
LocationInner mitochondrial membrane
InputNADH + FADH₂ (from glycolysis, link reaction, Krebs) + O₂
OutputThe bulk of ATP (~26–28 of the ~30–32 per glucose) + water
Oxygen needed?YES — absolutely (O₂ is the final electron acceptor)
PurposeConvert the energy in NADH/FADH₂ into ATP
The ATP tally (per glucose): glycolysis (2) + Krebs GTP (2) + oxidative phosphorylation (~26–28) = ~30–32 ATP total — showing that oxidative phosphorylation makes the vast majority (glycolysis alone gives only 2).
How It Works — the two coupled processes (core concept)
Oxidative phosphorylation = two linked steps:
Step 1 — The electron transport chain (builds the proton gradient)
  • NADH + FADH₂ donate electrons to a series of protein complexes (I–IV) in the inner mitochondrial membrane
  • As electrons pass down the chain (losing energy), that energy is used to pump protons (H⁺) out of the matrix → builds an electrochemical gradient (the "proton-motive force")
  • Oxygen is the final electron acceptor at the end of the chain (Complex IV): electrons + H⁺ + O₂ → water
  • This is why we need oxygen: without O₂ to accept the electrons, the whole chain backs up and stops (and NADH/FADH₂ can't be reoxidised → Krebs cycle stops too)
Step 2 — Chemiosmosis (makes the ATP)
  • The protons flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase (Complex V) → the flow drives the enzyme to make ATP from ADP + Pi
  • The principle (chemiosmotic theory): the energy isn't transferred directly — it's stored as a proton gradient, then "cashed in" by letting protons flow back through ATP synthase (like water through a turbine)
Why Oxygen Is Essential — the key concept
  • Oxygen's only metabolic job is to be the final electron acceptor at the end of the chain
  • No oxygen → the chain stops → no proton gradient → no ATP from oxidative phosphorylation, AND NADH/FADH₂ can't be reoxidised → NAD⁺/FAD run out → Krebs cycle + link reaction halt
The consequence (ties the metabolism notes together): without O₂, the cell is left with only anaerobic glycolysis → lactate (2 ATP) → lactic acidosis (cross-ref glycolysis) — this is the biochemical basis of why hypoxia/ischaemia causes lactic acidosis and rapid energy failure.

Overview — Gluconeogenesis & Glycogen Metabolism
📷 Image placeholder — glucose storage and production — glycogenesis/glycogenolysis (liver vs muscle) and gluconeogenesis from lactate, alanine and glycerol, with the Cori cycle recycling muscle/RBC lactate through the liver
These two pathways handle glucose storage and production — glycogen is the body's short-term glucose store, and gluconeogenesis makes new glucose from non-carbohydrate sources when stores run low.
The organising principle: the body must keep blood glucose constant (the brain depends on it), so it has a tiered system — glycogen first (hours), then gluconeogenesis (longer fasting) — controlled by the insulin/glucagon balance. These are the glucose-raising pathways (opposing glycolysis).
Why it matters: underpins the fasting response, hypoglycaemia, diabetes, glycogen storage diseases, and how metformin works — cross-ref glycolysis (the reverse), glucose homeostasis (insulin/glucagon), the fed/fasted state, diabetes, liver function.
Glycogen Metabolism — the short-term store
Glycogen = the storage form of glucose (a branched glucose polymer), stored mainly in liver + muscle:
Liver glycogen Muscle glycogen
PurposeMaintains blood glucose (for the whole body, esp. brain)Local fuel for muscle contraction only
Key differenceCan release glucose into the bloodCannot release glucose into blood (lacks glucose-6-phosphatase)
The two processes
  • Glycogenesis (storage): glucose → glycogen, when glucose is plentiful — stimulated by insulin (fed state)
  • Glycogenolysis (breakdown): glycogen → glucose, when glucose is needed — stimulated by glucagon + adrenaline (fasting/stress)
The liver-vs-muscle point: only the liver can release glucose into the blood (it has glucose-6-phosphatase); muscle glycogen stays local (fuels that muscle, can't raise blood glucose) — which is why liver glycogen is the blood-glucose buffer.
Timescale: liver glycogen is the main glucose source for roughly the first 12 hours and is largely exhausted by about 24 hours; gluconeogenesis takes over progressively and dominates by ~24 hours.
Gluconeogenesis — making new glucose
  • Definition: synthesis of new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors — essentially glycolysis run in reverse (with workarounds for the irreversible steps)
  • Where: mainly the liver (and some kidney)
  • When: continuously, but its share rises as fasting progresses — it already supplies roughly a third to a half of the liver's glucose output after an overnight fast, and becomes the sole source once glycogen is exhausted, keeping the brain and red cells (obligate glucose users) supplied
The precursors (the substrates):
Precursor Source
LactateFrom anaerobic glycolysis (the Cori cycle — muscle/RBC lactate → liver → glucose)
Amino acids (esp. alanine)From muscle protein breakdown (the major gluconeogenic substrate in starvation)
GlycerolFrom fat (triglyceride) breakdown
The key point — what can't make glucose: fatty acids cannot be converted to glucose (acetyl-CoA can't go back to pyruvate) → so in starvation, the body can't make glucose from fat directly → instead it makes ketones from fat (cross-ref ketogenesis) to spare glucose.
The Cori Cycle — the lactate recycling loop
  • The loop: exercising muscle/RBCs do anaerobic glycolysis → lactate → travels to the liver → gluconeogenesis converts lactate → glucose → returns to the muscle
The purpose: recycles lactate (preventing lactic acidosis) + shifts the metabolic burden to the liver → lets muscle keep producing ATP anaerobically while the liver regenerates glucose.
Hormonal Control — the insulin/glucagon switch
These pathways are reciprocally controlled with glycolysis by the insulin:glucagon ratio:
State Hormone Glycogen Gluconeogenesis
Fed (high insulin)InsulinGlycogenesis (store)Off
Fasted (high glucagon)Glucagon (+ adrenaline, cortisol)Glycogenolysis (release)On
The logic: insulin = "store glucose" (glycogenesis, ↓gluconeogenesis); glucagon = "make/release glucose" (glycogenolysis → gluconeogenesis).
Cortisol + adrenaline also drive gluconeogenesis (counter-regulatory — why stress/steroids ↑glucose; cross-ref adrenal + glucose homeostasis).
The Fasting Timeline — putting it together
The body's glucose-supply strategy as fasting progresses:
  • Hours: liver glycogenolysis (glycogen stores)
  • ~12–24h+: stores depleted → gluconeogenesis (from lactate, amino acids, glycerol)
  • Prolonged starvation: ketogenesis (fat → ketones) becomes the main fuel → spares glucose + protein (cross-ref) — the brain adapts to use ketones
(This is the fasted-state progression that the fed/fasted note covers in full.)

Overview — Fatty Acid Oxidation & Ketogenesis
📷 Image placeholder — fatty-acid oxidation and ketogenesis — lipolysis → free fatty acids → carnitine shuttle into mitochondria → β-oxidation to acetyl-CoA; when acetyl-CoA overwhelms the Krebs cycle the liver makes the ketone bodies acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate and acetone
When glucose is scarce, the body switches to burning fat — fatty acids are oxidised for energy, and the liver converts some into ketones as an alternative fuel (especially for the brain).
The organising principle: fat is the body's large, long-term energy store, mobilised in the fasted state; β-oxidation breaks fatty acids into acetyl-CoA (→ Krebs → ATP), and when this overwhelms the system (or glucose is very low), the liver makes ketones. The whole system is switched on by low insulin / high glucagon.
Why it matters: the direct physiology behind DKA, starvation ketosis, the fasting fuel switch, and why fat can't make glucose — cross-ref glucose homeostasis (insulin/glucagon), gluconeogenesis (the "fat can't make glucose" point), Krebs cycle (acetyl-CoA destination), DKA, the fed/fasted state.
Why and When Fat Is Burned — the context
  • Fat (triglyceride) is the major energy store — far larger than glycogen (weeks of energy vs ~a day) and energy-dense
  • Mobilised in the fasted/starved state: low insulin + high glucagon/adrenaline → lipolysis (adipose triglyceride → free fatty acids + glycerol) → fatty acids travel (albumin-bound) to tissues to be burned
The glycerol point: the glycerol from lipolysis can enter gluconeogenesis (→ glucose), but the fatty acids cannot make glucose (cross-ref) → they're burned for energy or made into ketones.
β-oxidation — burning fatty acids (the core)
  • Definition: fatty acids are broken down two carbons at a time → each cycle releases acetyl-CoA + NADH + FADH₂
  • Where: the mitochondria (matrix)
The carnitine shuttle
  • Long-chain fatty acids can't cross the inner mitochondrial membrane alone → they need the carnitine shuttle (carnitine palmitoyltransferase, CPT) to get in
The clinical link: fatty-acid oxidation defects → can't oxidise fat → hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and weakness on fasting. MCAD deficiency is the one to know — it is on the NHS newborn blood spot screen.
The yield: β-oxidation produces lots of acetyl-CoA + NADH + FADH₂ → the acetyl-CoA enters the Krebs cycle → oxidative phosphorylation → abundant ATP (fat is very energy-rich) — cross-ref Krebs + ox-phos.
The regulation: β-oxidation is inhibited by insulin (fed) and stimulated by glucagon (fasted) → fat is burned only when glucose is scarce.
Ketogenesis — making ketones
  • When: in prolonged fasting, starvation, or uncontrolled diabetes — when fat is being burned rapidly and/or glucose is very low
The mechanism (the key concept)
  • Rapid β-oxidation floods the liver with acetyl-CoA, but the Krebs cycle can't keep up (oxaloacetate is depleted — diverted to gluconeogenesis) → excess acetyl-CoA is converted by the liver into ketone bodies:
  • Acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate (the two main ketones), + acetone (the volatile one → fruity breath)
The purpose (why ketones matter): ketones are a water-soluble, exportable fuel that the brain can use (the brain can't burn fatty acids directly, but it can use ketones) → in starvation, ketones become the brain's main fuel → spares glucose and protein (less need for gluconeogenesis from muscle breakdown).
The liver makes them but can't use them (lacks the enzyme) → it exports ketones to other tissues (brain, muscle, heart).
The Fasting Fuel Switch — the integrating timeline
How fuel use shifts as fasting progresses (ties together the metabolism notes):
  • Fed: glucose (glycolysis), store glycogen + fat
  • Early fasting (hours): glycogenolysis (liver glycogen)
  • Fasting (~12–24h onwards): gluconeogenesis + β-oxidation of fat (most tissues switch to fat)
  • Prolonged starvation: ketogenesis → ketones fuel the brain → spares glucose + muscle protein (the adaptive endpoint)
The key adaptation: as starvation continues, the brain shifts from glucose to ketones → dramatically reduces the need to break down muscle for gluconeogenesis (protein-sparing).

The DKA mechanism (the payoff — cross-ref): in type 1 diabetes, absolute insulin deficiency → (1) hyperglycaemia (no glucose uptake) + (2) unrestrained lipolysis → massive β-oxidation → massive ketogenesis → ketones (acids) accumulate → high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (cross-ref acid-base) + osmotic diuresis/dehydration.
  • The features fall out of the physiology: Kussmaul breathing (respiratory compensation for the acidosis), fruity breath (acetone), dehydration, ketones in urine/blood
The insulin point: insulin normally suppresses ketogenesis → its absence (T1DM) unleashes it; this is why DKA is typical of absolute insulin deficiency (T1DM). But DKA is not exclusive to T1DM — it also occurs in T2DM under severe stress, and as euglycaemic DKA in patients on SGLT2 inhibitors, where the glucose may be near-normal and ketones must be checked.

Overview — The Fed vs Fasted State
📷 Image placeholder — the fasting fuel-switch timeline — dietary glucose → liver glycogen (hours) → gluconeogenesis + β-oxidation (>16 h) → ketones in prolonged starvation, plotted against the falling insulin:glucagon ratio, with the brain switching from glucose to ketones (protein-sparing)
This note integrates all the metabolic pathways — glycolysis, glycogen, gluconeogenesis, fat oxidation, ketogenesis — into the two states the body cycles between: fed (absorptive) and fasted (post-absorptive).
The organising principle: the body switches between storing fuel (fed) and mobilising fuel (fasted), governed almost entirely by the insulin:glucagon ratio — high insulin = store, high glucagon = mobilise. Every pathway is coordinately switched on or off depending on the state.
Why it matters: the unifying framework that makes diabetes, DKA, starvation, and the metabolic response to stress/illness coherent — cross-ref glucose homeostasis (the hormones), and all the metabolism subtabs (glycolysis, glycogen/gluconeogenesis, fat oxidation/ketogenesis).
The Master Switch: Insulin vs Glucagon — the spine
The entire fed/fasted switch comes down to the insulin:glucagon ratio:
Fed (high insulin:glucagon) Fasted (low insulin:glucagon)
Dominant hormoneInsulinGlucagon (+ cortisol, adrenaline, GH)
Overall themeSTORE (anabolic)MOBILISE (catabolic)
TriggerAfter a meal (↑glucose)Between meals/overnight, fasting
The logic: insulin signals "fuel is plentiful → store it"; glucagon signals "fuel is scarce → release/make it". Every pathway below follows this switch.
The Fed (Absorptive) State — storing fuel (insulin dominant)
After a meal, glucose/amino acids/fats are absorbed → insulin rises → the body stores everything:
Tissue What happens (insulin-driven)
LiverGlycogenesis (store glycogen), lipogenesis (make fat); glycolysis on; gluconeogenesis OFF
MuscleGlucose uptake (GLUT4), glycogen + protein synthesis
AdiposeGlucose + fat uptake, triglyceride storage; lipolysis OFF
NetGlucose used + stored as glycogen/fat; blood glucose falls back to normal
The summary: fed state = glycolysis + glycogenesis + lipogenesis ON; gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, β-oxidation, ketogenesis OFF (no need to mobilise — insulin suppresses them all).
The Fasted (Post-absorptive) State — mobilising fuel (glucagon dominant)
Between meals, glucose falls → glucagon rises (+ adrenaline, cortisol) → the body mobilises stores to keep blood glucose up for the brain:
Tissue What happens (glucagon-driven)
LiverGlycogenolysis (release glucose) → then gluconeogenesis (make glucose from lactate/amino acids/glycerol) → also ketogenesis in prolonged fasting
MuscleSwitches to fatty acids for fuel (spares glucose for brain); breaks down protein → amino acids for gluconeogenesis
AdiposeLipolysis → free fatty acids + glycerol
NetMaintain blood glucose (for brain/RBCs) while most tissues burn fat
The summary: fasted state = glycogenolysis → gluconeogenesis → β-oxidation → ketogenesis ON; glycogenesis, lipogenesis, glycolysis (in liver) OFF.
The priority: protect the brain's glucose supply — so glucose is reserved for the brain while other tissues switch to fat.
The Fasting Timeline — the integrated progression
As fasting deepens, fuel sources shift in a defined sequence (pulling together all the metabolism notes):
Stage Time Main fuel source
Fed0–4hDietary glucose (+ storing the rest)
Early fasting4–12hLiver glycogen (glycogenolysis)
Fasting~12–24h to daysGluconeogenesis (lactate, amino acids, glycerol) + β-oxidation (fat for most tissues)
Prolonged starvationDays+Ketones (brain switches to ketones → spares glucose + protein)
The key adaptation (the elegant endpoint): as starvation progresses, the brain shifts from glucose to ketones → this drastically reduces gluconeogenesis from muscle protein → protein-sparing (preserving muscle for as long as possible).
The Brain's Special Status — why this all matters
  • The brain is an obligate glucose user in the short term (can't use fatty acids) → which is why the body works so hard to maintain blood glucose during fasting
  • But in prolonged starvation, the brain adapts to use ketones → the key metabolic adaptation to starvation — it spares muscle protein and so prolongs survival

Overview — Protein / Amino Acid Metabolism & the Urea Cycle
📷 Image placeholder — nitrogen handling and the urea cycle — transamination (ALT/AST) collecting amino groups onto glutamate → deamination releasing toxic ammonia → the hepatic urea cycle converting ammonia to urea for renal excretion
Proteins are broken down to amino acids, which can be used for synthesis, energy, or glucose — but their nitrogen produces toxic ammonia, which the liver must convert to urea for safe excretion.
The organising principle: amino acids are unique among fuels because they contain nitrogen — so their metabolism has two parts: handling the carbon skeleton (used for energy/glucose) and disposing of the nitrogen (→ ammonia → urea). The urea cycle is the liver's solution to the toxic-ammonia problem.
Why it matters: underpins hepatic encephalopathy, the protein breakdown of starvation/stress, inborn errors of metabolism, and why liver failure raises ammonia — cross-ref liver function (ammonia→urea, encephalopathy), gluconeogenesis (amino acids as substrate), fed/fasted state, the metabolism set.
Where Amino Acids Come From and Go — the overview
  • Sources: dietary protein + breakdown of body protein (esp. muscle, in fasting/stress)
Fates of amino acids (unlike glucose/fat, there's no dedicated storage form — excess is broken down):
Fate What happens
Protein synthesisBuilding new proteins (the priority)
EnergyCarbon skeleton → Krebs cycle → ATP
GlucoseGlucogenic amino acids → gluconeogenesis (cross-ref)
KetonesKetogenic amino acids → ketone bodies
Nitrogen disposalThe amino group → ammonia → urea
The key point: there's no storage form of protein — so excess amino acids must be broken down (you can't "store" them like glycogen/fat), and their nitrogen must be disposed of.
Handling the Nitrogen — the two-step process (the core problem)
Amino acids must have their nitrogen-containing amino group removed before the carbon skeleton can be used for energy/glucose:
Step Process What it does
1. TransaminationAmino group transferred to a keto-acid (→ glutamate)Collects nitrogen onto glutamate; uses ALT + AST (the transaminases)
2. DeaminationGlutamate releases the amino group as ammonia (NH₃)Frees the nitrogen as toxic ammonia → must be detoxified
The ALT/AST point: transamination uses alanine aminotransferase (ALT) + aspartate aminotransferase (AST) — the same enzymes measured as LFTs (they leak from damaged hepatocytes → ↑ in liver injury; cross-ref liver function).
The problem: deamination produces ammonia, which is highly neurotoxic → it can't be allowed to accumulate → the urea cycle solves this.
The Urea Cycle — the ammonia-disposal solution (the core)
  • Purpose: convert toxic ammonia → urea (non-toxic, water-soluble) for excretion by the kidneys
  • Where: the liver (the only organ with the full urea cycle)
  • The concept: ammonia (+ CO₂ + a second nitrogen from aspartate) is processed through a cyclical series of reactions → produces urea (which carries 2 nitrogen atoms out) → urea enters the blood → excreted by the kidneys in urine
You don't need the individual intermediates (ornithine, citrulline, arginine...) at MBBS depth — the key facts are: ammonia → urea, in the liver, excreted renally.
The regulation: the cycle ramps up with a high-protein diet and during fasting/starvation (when muscle protein is being broken down for gluconeogenesis → more nitrogen to dispose of).
When Ammonia Accumulates — the clinical synthesis
Ammonia rises when the urea cycle can't keep up — the two main scenarios:
Cause Mechanism
Liver failure / cirrhosisThe failing liver can't convert ammonia → urea → ↑ammonia → hepatic encephalopathy (cross-ref liver function)
Portosystemic shuntingBlood bypasses the liver (cirrhosis/shunts) → ammonia not detoxified → encephalopathy
Urea cycle enzyme defects (inborn errors)Inherited deficiency (e.g. OTC deficiency) → hyperammonaemia, esp. in neonates
Hepatic encephalopathy (the key clinical link — cross-ref): ↑ammonia crosses the blood-brain barrier → neurotoxicity → confusion, asterixis (flap), drowsiness, coma.
  • Treatment logic (derivable from the physiology): lactulose (acidifies the colon → traps ammonia as ammonium for excretion + speeds gut transit) is the mainstay for an acute episode; rifaximin (↓ammonia-producing gut bacteria) is added to lactulose to prevent recurrence of overt encephalopathy — cross-ref
The Carbon Skeletons — the other half
After the nitrogen is removed, the carbon skeleton is used:
  • Glucogenic amino acids (most, esp. alanine) → gluconeogenesis → glucose (cross-ref — the major gluconeogenic substrate in starvation)
  • Ketogenic amino acids (leucine, lysine) → acetyl-CoA/ketones
  • Or fed into the Krebs cycle for energy
The starvation link: in prolonged fasting, muscle protein is broken down → amino acids → (alanine) → gluconeogenesis → glucose for the brain → this is the protein breakdown that ketosis tries to minimise (cross-ref fed/fasted + ketogenesis).
Clinical Relevance — the payoff

ALT/AST as LFTsThe transamination enzymes → leak in hepatocyte damage

Overview — Drug Metabolism (Biotransformation)
📷 Image placeholder — the two phases of drug biotransformation — Phase I (CYP450 oxidation/reduction/hydrolysis) adding or exposing a reactive group, then Phase II conjugation (e.g. glucuronidation) attaching a polar group to make a water-soluble, excretable metabolite
Drug metabolism (biotransformation) = the body's chemical modification of drugs, mainly by the liver, to prepare them for elimination.
The organising principle: most drugs are lipophilic (so they can cross membranes/be absorbed) — but that same lipophilicity means the kidney can't excrete them (they'd be reabsorbed). So the body chemically converts them into water-soluble forms that can be excreted — done in two phases (I and II).
Why it matters: the biochemical foundation behind drug clearance, prodrugs, drug interactions (CYP450), pharmacogenomic variation, and hepatic drug handling — cross-ref PK/PD & drug interactions (the clinical application — not repeated here), liver function, renal/hepatic dose adjustment.
Why Drugs Need Metabolising — the core rationale
  • The problem: most drugs are lipid-soluble (needed for absorption + crossing membranes to reach their target) → but lipid-soluble substances are reabsorbed by the kidney (they cross back across the tubule) → so they can't be excreted as-is
  • The solution: the body makes drugs more water-soluble (polar) → then they can't be reabsorbed → excreted in urine (or bile)
The overarching purpose: biotransformation = lipophilic → hydrophilic → excretable.
The Two Phases — the spine
Drug metabolism occurs in two sequential phases (a drug may undergo one or both):
Phase I Phase II
Type of reactionCatabolic — oxidation, reduction, hydrolysisAnabolic — conjugation
What it doesAdds/exposes a reactive functional group (e.g. –OH)Attaches a large polar molecule to that group
Main enzymesCytochrome P450 (CYP450)Transferases (glucuronyl, sulfo, acetyl, methyl)
ProductSlightly more polar (sometimes still active/toxic)Highly water-soluble → excreted
The sequence logic: Phase I "unmasks/adds" a handle, then Phase II "attaches a water-soluble tag" to that handle → the conjugate is polar enough to excrete. Phase I often precedes Phase II, but Phase II can occur alone.
Phase I Metabolism — CYP450, the workhorse
  • The main reactions: oxidation (commonest), reduction, hydrolysis — these add or expose a functional group (–OH, –NH₂, –COOH)
  • The cytochrome P450 (CYP450) system: a family of liver (+ gut) enzymes responsible for most Phase I oxidation — the central drug-metabolising system
The key point — Phase I products aren't always "safer": the metabolite can be less active, equally active, more active, or toxic:
  • Prodrugs — Phase I activates them
  • Toxic metabolites — e.g. paracetamol → NAPQI (the hepatotoxic metabolite — cross-ref toxicology)
CYP450 is the basis of drug interactions (inducers/inhibitors) — the clinical detail is in your PK/PD note (cross-ref); here the point is just that CYP450 = the main Phase I enzyme system + the site of most interactions.
Phase II Metabolism — conjugation, the finisher
The reaction: attaching a large polar (water-soluble) molecule to the drug (or its Phase I metabolite):
Conjugation Adds
Glucuronidation (commonest)Glucuronic acid (e.g. bilirubin, morphine, paracetamol)
SulfationSulfate
AcetylationAcetyl group
MethylationMethyl group
Glutathione conjugationGlutathione (detoxifies reactive metabolites — e.g. NAPQI)
The result: conjugation usually produces an inactive, highly water-soluble product → readily excreted in urine/bile. Not always, though: morphine-6-glucuronide is an active metabolite that accumulates in renal impairment.
The glutathione point: glutathione conjugation detoxifies reactive metabolites — e.g. it neutralises NAPQI (the toxic paracetamol metabolite); in overdose, glutathione is depleted → NAPQI accumulates → hepatotoxicity → N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione (cross-ref toxicology) — the elegant link.
Prodrugs — metabolism as activation
Some drugs are given in an inactive form (prodrug) and activated by metabolism (usually Phase I):
Prodrug Activated to
CodeineMorphine (via CYP2D6)
EnalaprilEnalaprilat
ClopidogrelActive metabolite (via CYP — needs activation)
Azathioprine6-mercaptopurine
LevodopaDopamine (in the brain)
The codeine point (pharmacogenomic): codeine → morphine via CYP2D6 → poor metabolisers get no analgesia (can't activate it); ultra-rapid metabolisers get dangerous morphine levels (esp. risky in children/breastfeeding).
Variation in Drug Metabolism — pharmacogenomics + factors
Drug metabolism varies between people, which is why drug responses differ:
Factor Effect
Genetic (pharmacogenomics)Fast vs slow acetylators (isoniazid, hydralazine — slow acetylators get more side effects); CYP polymorphisms (CYP2D6 for codeine/many drugs)
AgeNeonates (immature enzymes — e.g. ↓glucuronidation) + elderly (↓metabolism)
Liver functionImpairment → ↓metabolism → accumulation (cross-ref hepatic dose adjustment)
Drug interactionsCYP450 induction/inhibition (cross-ref PK/PD)
OtherNutrition, alcohol, smoking
The acetylator point: people are genetically fast or slow acetylators → slow acetylators accumulate drugs like isoniazid (→ peripheral neuropathy) and hydralazine/procainamide (→ drug-induced lupus).
First-pass Metabolism — brief
  • Orally-absorbed drugs pass through the gut wall + liver before reaching the systemic circulation → can be heavily metabolised first → ↓oral bioavailability (e.g. GTN, morphine, propranolol)
  • Routes that bypass first-pass: sublingual, IV, transdermal, rectal (partly) — clinical detail in your PK/PD note (cross-ref)

Slow acetylatorsIsoniazid (neuropathy), hydralazine (drug-induced lupus)
Drug interactionsCYP450 induction/inhibition (cross-ref PK/PD)

LIVER__Drug-Induced Liver Injury (DILI):
Overview — Drug-Induced Liver Injury
DILI = liver injury caused by drugs, herbs or toxins — the commonest cause of acute liver failure in the UK, overwhelmingly from paracetamol overdose. Among idiosyncratic (non-paracetamol) DILI, antibiotics are the commonest drug class.
Fork 1 — Mechanism
  • Intrinsic — predictable, dose-dependent
  • Idiosyncratic — unpredictable, dose-independent
Fork 2 — Pattern of injury
  • Hepatocellular vs cholestatic vs mixed
  • Defined by the LFT pattern → points to the culprit drug
Cross-ref: acute liver failure (paracetamol the commonest cause — the NAC link), viral / autoimmune hepatitis (differentials to exclude), and cirrhosis (the chronic DILI endpoint).
Mechanism Fork — Intrinsic vs Idiosyncratic
Intrinsic (direct) Idiosyncratic
PredictabilityPredictable, dose-dependentUnpredictable, dose-independent
OnsetRapid (hours–days)Latency variable — typically weeks to months; with co-amoxiclav and flucloxacillin the jaundice often appears after the course has finished
Reproducible?Yes (in anyone)Only in susceptible individuals
ArchetypeParacetamolAntibiotics, anti-TB drugs
Other examplesAmiodarone, valproateFlucloxacillin, co-amoxiclav, isoniazid
Paracetamol is the most common cause of direct DILI and the commonest cause of acute liver failure in the UK. Idiosyncratic sub-types: immunoallergic (hypersensitivity — fever, rash, eosinophilia) vs metabolic.
Pattern Fork — The R-Ratio (Hepatocellular / Cholestatic / Mixed)
The pattern is classified by the relative ratio of ALT to ALP, each expressed as a multiple of its own upper limit of normal — the R-ratio.
Pattern Biochemistry Prognosis Typical culprits
Hepatocellular ↑↑ ALT/AST (hepatocyte destruction) Potentially worse Paracetamol, statins, isoniazid, methotrexate, valproate
Cholestatic ↑ ALP (± bilirubin) predominant Better Co-amoxiclav, flucloxacillin, erythromycin, anabolic/contraceptive steroids, chlorpromazine
Mixed Both raised Most favourable — ALF rare Phenytoin, sulfonamides
Cholestatic injury is common, and antibiotics are the usual culprits. Memory anchors: co-amoxiclav = the classic cholestatic (commonest cause of drug-induced cholestatic jaundice); anabolic steroids/OCP = bland cholestasis; paracetamol = hepatocellular (zone 3 necrosis).
Key Culprit Drugs
Pattern Drugs
HepatocellularParacetamol, statins, anti-TB (isoniazid / rifampicin / pyrazinamide), methotrexate, valproate, amiodarone, NSAIDs
CholestaticCo-amoxiclav (commonest), flucloxacillin, macrolides (erythromycin), anabolic steroids, OCP, chlorpromazine, sulfonylureas

Paracetamol — The Archetype

📷 Image placeholder — paracetamol hepatotoxicity histology — zone 3 (centrilobular) coagulative necrosis surrounding the central vein, with relative sparing of the periportal zone 1 hepatocytes
Mechanism & histology
  • Metabolised to the toxic metabolite NAPQI, which depletes glutathione and binds mitochondrial proteins → hepatocyte death
  • Histology: zone 3 (centrilobular) hepatocellular necrosis
  • Transaminases become very markedly raised once injury is established (often >1000 IU/L, sometimes far higher) — but they are typically normal at presentation, and the treatment decision rests on the timed paracetamol level, not the LFTs
Risk & treatment
  • Worse outcome with older age, excess alcohol, chronic liver disease (deplete glutathione / induce enzymes)
  • N-acetylcysteine (replenishes glutathione)
  • Cross-ref the acute liver failure note for the nomogram + King's College criteria
Clinical Features & Diagnosis
  • Presentation ranges from an asymptomatic transaminase rise to acute liver failure — fatigue, nausea, RUQ pain, jaundice, pruritus (cholestatic); ± fever/rash/eosinophilia (immunoallergic)
  • DILI is a diagnosis of exclusion: take a careful drug/herbal/OTC history (including the preceding ~3 months) and exclude viral hepatitis (including hepatitis E — the commonest acute viral hepatitis in the UK and the classic DILI mimic), autoimmune hepatitis, alcohol and biliary obstruction
  • Histology is non-specific; eosinophilia may indicate a better prognosis
Hy's law (the prognostic red flag): hepatocellular DILI with ALT >3× ULN and bilirubin >2× ULN, without a significant ALP rise and with no other cause found, carries about 10% mortality.
Management
Stop the offending drug — the single most important step; most cases resolve on withdrawal.
  • Supportive care; monitor LFTs to recovery
  • Specific antidote where one exists: NAC for paracetamol
  • Manage acute liver failure if it develops (NAC, transplant referral, King's College criteria)
  • Document the reaction, avoid re-exposure, and report (yellow card)

Intrinsic (predictable, dose-dependent — paracetamol) vs idiosyncratic (unpredictable, dose-independent, latency of weeks to months); and hepatocellular vs cholestatic vs mixed (by R-ratio).

LIVER__Viral Hepatitis A–E:
Overview — The Five Hepatitis Viruses
Five viruses causing liver inflammation. The two decisive forks that organise the whole topic are route of transmission and whether it becomes chronic. Acute infectious hepatitis is a notifiable disease (UKHSA).
Virus Genome Transmission Chronic? Vaccine Treatment
A RNA Faecal-oral No Yes Supportive
B DNA Blood / body fluids Yes — <5% of adults, ~90% of infants infected at birth Yes Supportive / antivirals
C RNA Blood Yes (75%) No Direct-acting antivirals (curative)
D RNA Only with B Yes (via B vaccine) Pegylated interferon-α
E RNA Faecal-oral No (usually) No Supportive
The organising rule: "the vowels (A & E) come from the bowels" — faecal-oral, acute, don't chronify. B, C, D are blood-borne and can go chronic. B is the only DNA virus; the rest are RNA.
Cross-ref: cirrhosis + HCC (the chronic endpoints of B/C), acute liver failure (fulminant hepatitis), and the non-viral causes (alcoholic / autoimmune hepatitis).
Presentation & the Hepatitic LFT Picture
Clinical presentation (shared)
  • Often asymptomatic, or non-specific
  • Abdominal pain, fatigue, flu-like illness
  • Pruritus, myalgia / arthralgia
  • Nausea / vomiting, jaundice
The "hepatitic picture" on LFTs
  • ↑↑ transaminases (AST/ALT) with proportionally less rise in ALP
  • Transaminases = hepatocellular inflammation
  • Bilirubin rises → jaundice
  • Contrast the cholestatic picture (↑ ALP) of the biliary diseases
Hepatitis A — Faecal-Oral, Acute, Self-Limiting
RNA virus; faecal-oral — via contaminated food/water and person-to-person spread (household and sexual contacts); vaccine available. Relatively uncommon in the UK.
  • Close contacts are offered vaccine (± immunoglobulin) after exposure (UKHSA)
  • Can cause cholestasis — pruritus, significant jaundice, dark urine, pale stools
  • Diagnosis: IgM antibodies to hepatitis A (IgM anti-HAV)
  • Usually resolves without treatment — supportive + analgesia
  • Rarely → acute liver failure (fulminant hepatitis)
Hepatitis B — The DNA Virus & the Serology
Double-stranded DNA virus; transmitted by blood / body fluids — sexual contact, needle sharing (IVDU, tattoos), toothbrushes/razors, and vertical (mother-to-child).
Course
  • Most adults recover fully
  • Chronicity is strongly age-dependent: under 5% of infected adults become chronic carriers, but around 90% of infants infected at birth do — which is why the UK immunises babies of infected mothers
The viral markers
Marker Meaning
HBsAg (surface antigen)Active infection (acute or chronic)
HBeAg (e antigen)Active replication → high infectivity
HBcAb (core antibody)Past OR current infection (exposure)
HBsAb (surface antibody)Immunity — vaccination or past infection
HBV DNADirect viral load
Interpreting the picture
  • Screening = HBcAb (previous) + HBsAg (active); if positive → test HBeAg + HBV DNA
  • HBcAb IgM = active/acute; IgG = past infection (with HBsAg negative)
  • HBeAg positive = actively replicating, highly infectious; HBeAg negative + HBeAb positive = usually lower replication and infectivity — confirm with HBV DNA
The vaccination discriminator: vaccination injects HBsAg, so it gives HBsAb only. Isolated HBsAb = vaccinated; HBsAb + HBcAb = past natural infection.

📷 Image placeholder — serological course of chronic hepatitis B — HBsAg persists beyond 6 months and anti-HBs never appears; anti-HBc IgG persists, distinguishing chronic infection from the vaccinated (isolated anti-HBs) picture
Vaccination
  • Inject recombinant HBsAg; anti-HBs response is checked only in at-risk groups (healthcare workers, renal patients, babies of infected mothers)
  • Part of the UK 6-in-1 schedule. All pregnant women in the UK are screened for hepatitis B (NHS), and babies of infected mothers are vaccinated at birth, with hepatitis B immunoglobulin where the mother is highly infectious (UKHSA)
Management
  • Screen at-risk patients + for co-infections (HIV, hep A/C/D)
  • Refer to specialist; avoid alcohol; education + contact tracing
  • FibroScan (cirrhosis) + USS (HCC) surveillance
  • Antivirals to slow progression / reduce infectivity; transplant for fulminant failure
Hepatitis C — Blood-Borne, Curable
RNA virus, blood-borne — injecting drug use with shared equipment is the commonest route in the UK; sexual transmission is uncommon. No vaccine.
Course & complications
  • 1 in 4 clear it; 3 in 4 develop chronic hepatitis C
  • Complications: cirrhosis + its complications, and HCC
Testing
  • Hepatitis C antibody = screening
  • HCV RNA confirms diagnosis + gives viral load & genotype
The success story: now curable with direct-acting antivirals (e.g. sofosbuvir/velpatasvir), given over 8–12 weeks — curing >90%.
Hepatitis D — The B-Dependent One
  • RNA virus that can only survive in patients who also have hepatitis B — it attaches to HBsAg and cannot survive without it
  • Very low rates in the UK; increases the complications + disease severity of hepatitis B
  • Specialist treatment — historically pegylated interferon-α, with limited efficacy and significant side effects; a specific antiviral is now available (NICE)
The hepatitis B vaccine protects against D by preventing B (D cannot exist without B).
Hepatitis E — Usually Mild, but Watch Pregnancy
  • RNA virus, faecal-oral, now the commonest cause of acute viral hepatitis in the UK (genotype 3, zoonotic from undercooked pork/game)
  • Usually a mild illness, cleared within weeks, no treatment needed; no routine vaccine in the UK
  • Rarely progresses to chronic hepatitis + liver failure, usually in immunocompromised patients
Classically dangerous in pregnancy in endemic areas (genotype 1) — high mortality from acute liver failure. UK-acquired genotype 3 does not carry this risk.

LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis:
Overview — Compensated vs Decompensated
Cirrhosis = hepatocyte necrosis → fibrosis + nodule formation → impaired function + distorted architecture → portal hypertension. The decisive fork is compensated vs decompensated. Decompensation = the triad that kills.
Compensated cirrhosis
  • Portal hypertension present but no overt clinical events
  • Patient may be asymptomatic for years
  • 5-year survival ~80%
  • Goal: prevent decompensation (treat cause, surveillance)
Decompensated cirrhosis
  • Encephalopathy
  • Ascites (commonest event)
  • Variceal haemorrhage
  • ± SBP, hepatorenal syndrome, jaundice
  • 5-year survival ~20%; transplant referral
Aetiology
Common causes
  • Alcohol — most common in UK
  • Hepatitis B & C — most common worldwide
  • NAFLD — fastest growing cause
Rarer causes — screen for these
  • Autoimmune hepatitis — ANA, anti-SMA, ↑IgG
  • Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) — anti-mitochondrial Ab (AMA)
  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) — p-ANCA, associated with IBD
  • Haemochromatosis — ↑ferritin, ↑transferrin sat, HFE gene
  • Wilson's disease — ↓caeruloplasmin, Kayser-Fleischer rings
  • α1-antitrypsin deficiency — PiZZ phenotype
Clinical Features — Stigmata of Chronic Liver Disease

  • Na⁺ — hyponatraemia = severe disease (impaired free-water clearance)
  • AFP — may be raised in chronic liver disease and in HCC, but it is neither sensitive nor specific; a rising AFP prompts imaging rather than making the diagnosis
  • Non-invasive liver screen: viral hepatitis serology, ANA/SMA/AMA/p-ANCA, ferritin + transferrin sat, caeruloplasmin, α1-AT level
Imaging & scoring
  • USS liver — nodular surface, ascites, splenomegaly, portal vein diameter, Doppler flow
  • FibroScan (transient elastography) — first-line non-invasive test to diagnose cirrhosis (NICE)
  • Liver biopsy — the reference standard; reserved for when non-invasive tests are equivocal or the cause is unclear
  • OGD — offered after a diagnosis of cirrhosis to look for oesophageal varices, unless the patient is starting a non-selective β-blocker. If no varices and not on a β-blocker, repeat every 3 years (NICE)

Portal Hypertension
Portal vein = 75% of hepatic inflow. Portal pressure is measured indirectly as the hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG; normal 1–5 mmHg). HVPG >10 mmHg = clinically significant portal hypertension — varices form and prophylaxis is considered. HVPG >12 mmHg is the threshold above which varices bleed.

Variceal Haemorrhage

Acute upper GI bleed from ruptured oesophageal/gastric varices. 30-day mortality up to 20%. Resuscitate rapidly and treat simultaneously.
1
Resuscitate
Large-bore IV ×2, bloods + cross-match, IV fluids/blood. Avoid over-transfusion (↑portal pressure). Target Hb 70–80 g/L.

Vasopressin analogue → splanchnic vasoconstriction → ↓portal inflow. Start as soon as a variceal bleed is suspected; stop after haemostasis or at 5 days. Particular care — not an absolute bar — in ischaemic heart, peripheral vascular and respiratory disease; monitor sodium. If unsuitable, octreotide is used off-licence in the UK.
→
3

IV broad-spectrum antibiotics at presentation per local policy (commonly ceftriaxone) — they reduce infection and mortality. Give before or at endoscopy.
→

Band ligation is the treatment of choice for oesophageal varices. Bleeding gastric varices are injected with cyanoacrylate glue, with TIPS if that fails.
If ligation fails — salvage

  • TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) — for re-bleed; creates portal-hepatic shunt → ↓portal pressure. Risk: precipitates encephalopathy
  • Oesophageal transection (last resort)
Prevention
  • Primary prevention (before any bleed): for clinically significant portal hypertension (HVPG >10 mmHg, or varices seen at OGD), carvedilol is first choice, propranolol if carvedilol is unsuitable; band ligation if β-blockers are not tolerated (NICE). Start low and titrate; avoid carvedilol in severe hepatic impairment or refractory ascites
  • Secondary prevention (after a bleed): a non-selective β-blocker — ↓cardiac output + splanchnic vasoconstriction → ↓portal pressure; start after the acute bleed settles
  • Repeat band ligation every 2 weeks until varices obliterated
  • Consider TIPS for those who rebleed on propranolol + banding
Ascites
Mechanism: portal HTN → splanchnic vasodilation → ↓effective circulating volume → RAAS + SNS activation → Na⁺/water retention. Hypoalbuminaemia → ↓oncotic pressure → fluid into peritoneum.

Na⁺ restriction
A no-added-salt diet, roughly 5–6.5 g salt (about 90–110 mmol sodium) daily. Do not restrict more tightly — it worsens hyponatraemia and malnutrition. Avoid NSAIDs (worsen Na retention + AKI).

100 mg OD → titrate up to 400 mg. Aldosterone antagonist. Add furosemide if needed (ratio 100:40). Monitor U&E for hyperkalaemia and rising creatinine; stop diuretics in AKI, hyponatraemia or encephalopathy.
→

For tense ascites. Give 20% albumin (6–8 g per litre drained) to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction.
→
4

For refractory ascites. ↓Portal pressure → reduces formation. Risk: encephalopathy.
Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP)
A common and often silent complication of cirrhotic ascites, and substantially more frequent in hospitalised patients. Suspect in any cirrhotic patient with ascites who deteriorates — fever, abdominal pain, encephalopathy, or unexplained clinical worsening. Most common organism: E. coli.
Diagnosis & treatment
  • Ascitic tap: neutrophils >250 cells/mm³ → treat immediately (don't wait for culture)
  • Empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics per local policy — commonly piperacillin-tazobactam, or a third-generation cephalosporin such as cefotaxime — for 5 days
  • 20% albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 + 1 g/kg on day 3 → reduces hepatorenal syndrome risk
Prophylaxis & referral
  • Long-term oral ciprofloxacin after an episode of SBP (secondary prophylaxis). Norfloxacin appears in older texts but is no longer available in the UK
  • Primary prophylaxis: oral ciprofloxacin if ascitic protein is 15 g/L or less, until the ascites resolves (NICE). Observe fluoroquinolone safety restrictions and counsel on tendon and neurological side effects (MHRA)
  • SBP = indication for liver transplant referral
Hepatic Encephalopathy
Mechanism: toxins (principally ammonia from gut bacterial metabolism of proteins) bypass the diseased liver → reach the brain → astrocyte swelling + neurotransmitter disruption.
Clinical features
  • Grade 1–2: irritability, confusion, sleep disturbance, slurred speech
  • Grade 3–4: drowsiness → coma
  • Asterixis (flapping tremor — hold hands outstretched)
  • Fetor hepaticus (sweet musty breath — dimethyl sulphide)
  • Constructional apraxia (can't draw a 5-pointed star)
  • ↑Tone, hyperreflexia in acute; identify precipitant
Management — reduce gut ammonia
  • Lactulose — osmotic purgative → ↓colonic pH → ↓ammonia-producing bacteria + ↓ammonia absorption. Target 2–3 soft stools/day.
  • Rifaximin — added to lactulose to reduce recurrence of overt encephalopathy (NICE); it reduces ammonia-producing gut flora
  • Identify + treat precipitant: GI bleed, infection, constipation, dehydration, sedatives/opioids, electrolyte disturbance, over-diuresis
  • Confusion in cirrhosis is not automatically encephalopathy — check a capillary glucose, screen for sepsis, and consider Wernicke's, alcohol withdrawal and (in a coagulopathic patient who has fallen) a subdural haematoma
  • Adequate nutrition (high protein diet does NOT worsen encephalopathy)
Hepatorenal Syndrome
AKI in advanced liver disease — diagnosis of exclusion. Mechanism: splanchnic vasodilation → ↓effective circulating volume → RAAS activation → renal vasoconstriction → ↓GFR. No intrinsic renal pathology.
Diagnosis
  • Rising creatinine meeting AKI criteria, in cirrhosis with ascites
  • No sustained improvement after stopping diuretics and 2 days of IV 20% albumin (1 g/kg/day)
  • No shock
  • A very low urine Na⁺ is typical, but is no longer a diagnostic criterion
  • No other cause of AKI (infection, nephrotoxins, obstruction)
  • Urine microscopy: bland (no casts or cells)
Management
  • Terlipressin (splanchnic vasoconstriction → ↑renal perfusion), in a monitored setting. Check respiratory status first — do not start if hypoxic or with worsening breathlessness — and monitor for respiratory failure and infection during treatment (MHRA)
  • 20% albumin volume expansion (1 g/kg/day)
  • Stop nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, gentamicin, contrast)
  • TIPS in selected patients
  • Poor prognosis without liver transplantation — refer urgently
Cirrhosis Care Bundle (First 24 Hours)
The decompensated cirrhosis care bundle (BSG) is a checklist applied within the first 24 hours of any admission with decompensated cirrhosis (new/worsening ascites, variceal bleed, encephalopathy or jaundice). It standardises the early response and reduces preventable mortality.
1 · Investigate & confirm
  • Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFTs, CRP, clotting, glucose, VBG + lactate
  • Full septic screen (blood + urine cultures, CXR)
  • USS abdomen + Doppler — exclude portal vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari, HCC
2 · Ascitic tap within 24 h
  • Diagnostic paracentesis to exclude SBP — neutrophils >250 → treat at once (IV broad-spectrum antibiotics per local policy + 20% albumin)
  • Do NOT delay for deranged clotting — coagulopathy is not a contraindication
3 · Alcohol & thiamine
  • Assess withdrawal risk; a symptom-triggered benzodiazepine regimen (e.g. CIWA-Ar). In decompensated cirrhosis prefer lorazepam or oxazepam — chlordiazepoxide and diazepam accumulate and can deepen encephalopathy
  • IV thiamine and B-vitamin replacement before any glucose-containing fluid — prevents Wernicke's
4 · GI bleed / varices
  • Suspected variceal bleed → terlipressin + prophylactic IV broad-spectrum antibiotics per local policy (commonly ceftriaxone)
  • Restrictive transfusion target Hb 70–80 g/L; OGD + band ligation within 24 h
5 · Renal / AKI & HRS
  • Baseline + daily U&E; avoid nephrotoxics (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast)
  • Human albumin for SBP, large-volume paracentesis and hepatorenal syndrome
6 · Encephalopathy
  • Find & treat the precipitant (infection, GI bleed, constipation, dehydration, sedatives, electrolytes)
  • Lactulose (2–3 soft stools/day) ± rifaximin; avoid sedatives
Escalate early: senior / gastroenterology review, nutritional support, and consider referral to a specialist liver unit. Reassess against the bundle at 24 hours.
Three classic bundle traps: (1) withholding the ascitic tap for deranged clotting; (2) over-transfusing a variceal bleed (raises portal pressure); (3) giving glucose before thiamine.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Decompensation = encephalopathy + ascites + varices
Any one of these marks the transition. 5-year survival drops from 80% → 20%.
Stigmata by mechanism
↑Oestrogen → spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia. Synthetic → bruising, leukonychia. Portal HTN → caput medusae, ascites, splenomegaly.
PT + albumin = best function markers
LFTs may be normal in cirrhosis. FibroScan is the first-line non-invasive test for cirrhosis; biopsy is the reference standard.
Child-Pugh ABCDE
Albumin · Bilirubin · Clotting · Dilation (ascites) · Encephalopathy. Class C = worst. UK transplant listing uses UKELD (bilirubin, creatinine, INR, sodium).
HCC surveillance = 6-monthly ultrasound (± AFP)
AFP alone neither confirms nor excludes HCC. OGD after diagnosis, then every 3 years if no varices and not on a β-blocker.
Variceal bleed: terlipressin + abx + band ligation
Terlipressin needs caution, not an absolute bar, in ischaemic heart disease. Prophylactic antibiotics at presentation reduce infection and mortality. Carvedilol first choice for primary prevention; β-blocker + repeat banding after a bleed.
SAAG >11 = portal hypertension
Ascites management: Na restriction → spironolactone → paracentesis + albumin → TIPS.
Give albumin after large paracentesis
6–8 g per litre drained. Prevents post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction.
SBP: neutrophils >250 → treat at once
Don't wait for culture. E. coli most common. Ciprofloxacin for prophylaxis. SBP = transplant referral indication.
Encephalopathy: lactulose + rifaximin
Ammonia-driven. Asterixis + fetor hepaticus + constructional apraxia. Find the precipitant (bleed/infection/constipation).
Hepatorenal: AKI with no response to albumin
No improvement after stopping diuretics and 2 days of albumin. Terlipressin + albumin. Diagnosis of exclusion. Poor prognosis without transplant.
Budd-Chiari = post-hepatic portal HTN
Hepatic vein thrombosis. Tender hepatomegaly + ascites + no cirrhosis. Anticoagulate + TIPS.
LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disease:
Overview — The Stepwise Progression
Result of chronic excessive alcohol consumption. The defining principle: damage is reversible early, irreversible late.
1
Hepatic steatosis
Fatty liver. Reversible with abstinence. Often asymptomatic.
→
2
Alcoholic hepatitis
Inflammation + ballooning degeneration. Partly reversible. Can be acute-on-chronic.
→
3
Cirrhosis
Irreversible fibrosis + nodular regeneration. Portal hypertension, liver failure.
Recommended Limits & Units
UK guidelines (UK Chief Medical Officers)
  • ≤14 units/week for both men and women
  • Spread over 3+ days — not saved up for one session
  • No daily unit limit is set — the weekly guideline replaced the old daily benchmarks
  • Several drink-free days a week if cutting down
  • In pregnancy, or when trying to conceive, the safest approach is not to drink at all
Binge drinking & unit calculation
  • Binge (UK statistical definition) = more than 6 units in a single session for women, more than 8 units for men
  • Unit formula: (ABV% × volume in mL) ÷ 1000
  • Examples: 1 pint (568 mL) of 4% lager = 2.3 units; 250 mL of 13% wine = 3.3 units; 25 mL of 40% spirits = 1 unit
Clinical Features
Acute intoxication / dependency signs
  • Smelling of alcohol
  • Slurred speech, ataxia, drowsiness
  • Bloodshot eyes
  • Facial telangiectasia (dilated capillaries — chronic)
  • Tremor (withdrawal or chronic cerebellar)
  • Nausea, vomiting, anorexia
Alcoholic hepatitis — acute presentation
  • Jaundice (↑ bilirubin), RUQ pain, fever
  • Hepatomegaly (tender)
  • Ascites in severe cases
  • Can be severe or fatal — severe alcohol-related hepatitis carries a high short-term mortality
  • Stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, Dupuytren's) → see Liver Cirrhosis note
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — hepatic steatosis on ultrasound — a diffusely bright (hyperechoic) liver that is brighter than the adjacent renal cortex, with posterior beam attenuation
Bloods — the alcohol pattern
  • ↑MCV (macrocytosis) — direct toxicity + B-vitamin deficiency
  • ↑GGT — characteristically elevated and sensitive, but not specific: it also rises with cholestasis, metabolic fatty liver disease, obesity and enzyme-inducing drugs
  • ↑AST, ↑ALT — AST:ALT ratio ≥2:1 suggests alcoholic liver disease (in viral hepatitis / NAFLD, ALT > AST)
  • ↑ALP, ↑bilirubin (hepatitis/cirrhosis)
  • ↓Albumin, ↑PT/INR = impaired synthetic function
  • ↓Platelets (portal hypertension → hypersplenism)
  • U&Es (electrolyte disturbance common)
Other investigations
  • USS liver — steatosis (bright echogenic liver), cirrhosis (nodular), ascites, portal vein diameter
  • Liver biopsy — the reference standard for histological stage (steatosis / hepatitis / fibrosis / cirrhosis); Mallory-Denk bodies in alcoholic hepatitis
  • FibroScan (transient elastography) — non-invasive fibrosis staging
  • Maddrey's discriminant function — a severity score derived from the prothrombin time and bilirubin. A score ≥32 indicates severe disease and identifies a corticosteroid candidate
Management
Alcoholic hepatitis (severe)
  • Prednisolone 40 mg/day for 28 days — if Maddrey's DF ≥32
  • Lille score at day 7 — if no improvement (score >0.45), stop steroids (no benefit)
  • Withhold corticosteroids until active infection or GI bleeding has been effectively treated — these are reasons to delay, not permanent bars (NICE)
  • Counsel the patient: corticosteroids improve survival at about 1 month but not at 3 months to 1 year, and increase the risk of serious infection in the first 3 months (NICE)
  • Pentoxifylline — no longer recommended: it does not improve survival
General management
  • Stop drinking — detox programme, psychological support (CBT, AA), relapse-prevention drugs (acamprosate, naltrexone, disulfiram)
  • Nutritional support: high-calorie, high-protein diet; NGT if unable to eat
  • Thiamine (B1) + B vitamins — parenteral (IV) high-potency B vitamins in hospital
  • Treat complications (ascites, encephalopathy, varices — see Cirrhosis note)
  • Liver transplantation: considered in decompensated cirrhosis. Sustained abstinence and engagement with alcohol services are central, but UK practice no longer applies a fixed 6-month rule before referral — refer and discuss early with the transplant centre
Alcohol Withdrawal — The Timeline
Mechanism: chronic alcohol ↓ GABA receptors + ↑ NMDA receptors (compensatory). Sudden withdrawal → unopposed CNS excitability → seizures and delirium tremens (a medical emergency).
Time after last drinkFeature
6–12 hoursTremor, sweating, headache, anxiety, craving, tachycardia, hypertension
12–24 hoursHallucinations (visual, auditory, tactile) — patient may be orientated (unlike DTs)
24–48 hoursGeneralised tonic-clonic seizures (withdrawal fits)
24–72 hoursDelirium tremens (DTs) — confusion, agitation, autonomic instability (↑HR, ↑BP, sweating, fever). A medical emergency, with significant mortality if untreated.
Management of withdrawal
  • Benzodiazepines — oral chlordiazepoxide in a reducing regimen over 5–7 days. In liver impairment use a benzodiazepine needing little hepatic metabolism (e.g. lorazepam) at reduced dose with close monitoring, and avoid benzodiazepines altogether in severe liver impairment (NICE)
  • For withdrawal seizures give a quick-acting benzodiazepine (e.g. lorazepam) to reduce further fits — do not use phenytoin for alcohol withdrawal seizures (NICE)
  • Offer admission for medically assisted withdrawal to anyone at high risk of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, with a lower threshold in frail, cognitively impaired or unsupported patients (NICE)
  • A symptom-triggered regimen (e.g. CIWA-Ar) to guide benzodiazepine dosing
  • Parenteral (IV) high-potency B vitamins (thiamine) — give before, or at the same time as, glucose-containing fluids; then oral thiamine
  • Correct electrolytes (↓K⁺, ↓Mg²⁺, ↓phosphate common)
  • Quiet environment, hydration, seizure precautions
Delirium tremens — emergency Rx
  • Oral lorazepam first-line; if symptoms persist or oral medication is declined, parenteral lorazepam (or haloperidol) (NICE)
  • Parenteral (IV) high-potency B vitamins (thiamine)
  • Correct autonomic instability (fluids, electrolytes)
  • HDU/ICU if severe
  • Do NOT use haloperidol alone — lowers seizure threshold
Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome
📷 Image placeholder — Wernicke’s encephalopathy on MRI — symmetrical T2/FLAIR high signal in the mammillary bodies, medial thalami and periaqueductal grey matter
Cause: Thiamine (B1) deficiency — people with alcohol dependence malabsorb thiamine and often have poor dietary intake. Give thiamine before, or at the same time as, glucose-containing fluids or feeding in any alcohol-dependent patient, because a carbohydrate load without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy (glucose metabolism depletes the remaining thiamine).
Wernicke's encephalopathy — ACUTE, reversible
  • Classic triad: Confusion + Oculomotor disturbance (ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus) + Ataxia
  • The full triad is present in only a minority — treat on clinical suspicion, without waiting for all three features
  • MRI: signal change in periaqueductal grey + mammillary bodies
  • Treat immediately with parenteral (IV) high-dose thiamine, continued for a minimum of 5 days, then oral thiamine (NICE)
Korsakoff syndrome — CHRONIC, irreversible
  • Consequence of untreated or recurrent Wernicke's
  • Anterograde amnesia (can't form new memories)
  • Retrograde amnesia (gaps in past memory)
  • Confabulation — unconscious fabrication of memories to fill gaps
  • Behavioural change, apathy
  • Irreversible — residential/nursing care often required
⭐ Exam Pearls
Steatosis → hepatitis → cirrhosis
Reversible → partly reversible → irreversible. Abstinence can halt progression at any stage.
≤14 units/week
Unit = (ABV% × mL) ÷ 1000. Binge = more than 6 units (women) / more than 8 units (men) in a session.
AST:ALT ≥2:1 = alcoholic
In viral hepatitis / MASLD: ALT > AST. GGT is characteristically high in alcohol use, but is sensitive rather than specific.
↑MCV + ↓albumin + ↑PT
Macrocytosis from B-vitamin deficiency. Low albumin + raised PT = failing synthetic function.
Maddrey's DF ≥32 → prednisolone
A severity score from PT and bilirubin. Review response with the Lille score at day 7.
Withdrawal timeline
Tremor (6–12 h) → Hallucinations (12–24 h) → Seizures (24–48 h) → DTs (24–72 h)
Mechanism: ↓GABA + ↑NMDA
Unopposed excitability on withdrawal. Treat with chlordiazepoxide (a benzodiazepine replaces GABA tone) — but prefer lorazepam in liver impairment.
DTs are a medical emergency
Confusion + agitation + autonomic storm. Oral lorazepam first-line + parenteral thiamine + HDU.
Wernicke's triad: COA
Confusion + Ophthalmoplegia + Ataxia. Acute, reversible. Only a minority have all three — treat on suspicion with parenteral thiamine.
Thiamine with or before glucose
A carbohydrate load without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's. Never delay glucose in hypoglycaemia — treat it at once and give thiamine alongside.
Korsakoff = irreversible amnesia
Anterograde + retrograde amnesia + confabulation. Consequence of untreated Wernicke's.
LIVER__Autoimmune Hepatitis:
Overview

Autoimmune-mediated hepatocyte inflammation of unknown aetiology causing chronic hepatitis that can progress to cirrhosis if untreated. Affects all ages but classically presents in young women.

Classic Associations
  • Other autoimmune conditions (thyroid disease, RA, IBD, coeliac)
  • Hypergammaglobulinaemia -- raised IgG (a diagnostic pillar)
  • HLA-B8 / DR3 and HLA-DR4 associations
  • Young woman + autoimmune history + raised IgG + ANA/SMA = classic picture
Distinguish from cholestatic autoimmune disease
  • PBC -- anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA), cholestatic LFTs, middle-aged women
  • PSC -- p-ANCA, bile duct beading on MRCP, associated with IBD
  • AIH = hepatitic (raised transaminases); PBC/PSC = cholestatic (raised ALP/GGT)
Types (Autoantibody Classification)
TypeKey antibodiesTypical patient
Type 1 ANA (antinuclear) and/or SMA (smooth muscle) Adults and children; commonest type
Type 2 Anti-LKM1 (liver-kidney microsomal type 1) and/or anti-LC1 (liver cytosol type 1) Mainly children and young adults (rarer in adults, but not confined to them)
Memory: T1 = ANA/SMA (all ages, commonest) | T2 = LKM1/LC1 (mainly children and young adults). Anti-SLA/LP is highly specific but sits within type 1
Clinical Features
Usual presentation (insidious)
  • Fatigue, malaise, anorexia
  • Nausea
  • Arthralgia
  • Signs of chronic liver disease if advanced (palmar erythema, spider naevi, hepatosplenomegaly)
Acute presentation (a substantial minority)
  • Fever, jaundice, acute hepatitis picture
  • Can mimic acute viral hepatitis
  • Rarely: acute liver failure
Amenorrhoea: recognised in active AIH and often resolves once remission is achieved. It reflects disturbed hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal function in chronic liver disease rather than a single well-defined mechanism
Investigations

  • Bilirubin raised in active disease
  • PT/INR, albumin (synthetic function)

  • Interface hepatitis ("piecemeal necrosis") -- inflammation extends beyond the limiting plate into the periportal area
  • Bridging necrosis -- necrosis spanning portal tracts
  • Plasma cell infiltrate (characteristic)
  • Rosette formation of hepatocytes
Interface hepatitis on biopsy + raised IgG + positive autoantibodies is the classic picture -- but none of the three is essential. Diagnosis also requires exclusion of viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, alcohol- and metabolic-associated liver disease and Wilson's disease before immunosuppression is started

1
Induce remission
Prednisolone ~0.5 mg/kg/day, usually not exceeding 40 mg/day, as a single morning dose
to
2
Taper prednisolone
Maintenance 5-15 mg/day
to
3

Part of first-line therapy, usually added at around 2 weeks. Check TPMT activity before starting (absent = do not give; intermediate = reduced dose). to

Young woman + other autoimmune disease + fatigue + raised IgG + ANA/SMA positive

LIVER__Haemochromatosis:
The decisive fork: iron deposition by organ. One disease — too much iron — and every clinical feature, investigation, and prognosis falls out of where the iron lands. HFE mutation → ↓hepcidin → unregulated gut iron absorption → iron loads into parenchymal organs over decades. Thalassaemia reaches the same organ-damage pattern by a different route: iron overload from inherited over-absorption here, versus transfusional loading there.
Overview
What is hereditary haemochromatosis?
  • Autosomal recessive disorder of iron metabolism
  • HFE gene, chromosome 6 — classic genotype: C282Y homozygosity. Penetrance is incomplete — many C282Y homozygotes never develop iron overload, so genotype alone does not make the diagnosis: raised transferrin saturation and ferritin must be present. H63D is a common variant that does not by itself cause significant iron overload
  • Excess total body iron → tissue deposition → organ damage
  • Primary (genetic) — not secondary to haemolysis or transfusion
Mechanism

HFE mutation → ↓hepcidin production → unregulated ferroportin activity → ↑gut iron absorption → iron loads into parenchymal cells over decades → oxidative damage → fibrosis/dysfunction

Onset typically after 40; later in women (menstrual iron loss offsets accumulation, so women typically present after the menopause)

Clinical Features — Iron Deposition by Organ
📷 Image placeholder — hand X-ray in haemochromatosis arthropathy — degenerative change with joint-space narrowing and characteristic hook-shaped osteophytes at the 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, plus chondrocalcinosis
Classic triad: “bronze diabetes” + hepatomegaly. Early triad: fatigue, arthralgia, erectile dysfunction.
OrganIron effectClinical feature
LiverDeposition → fibrosisHepatomegaly, cirrhosis, ↑risk of HCC

SkinMelanin + iron depositionBronze / slate-grey pigmentation

HeartMyocardial ironRestrictive physiology early (diastolic dysfunction), progressing to dilated cardiomyopathy; heart failure and arrhythmia
Pituitary/gonadsGonadotrophin deficiencyHypogonadotrophic hypogonadism — ED, ↓libido, infertility, amenorrhoea

📷 Image placeholder — Perl's Prussian blue stain of liver — hepatocellular iron (haemosiderin) deposition staining bright blue, confirming iron overload
Diagnostic sequence: Transferrin saturation → ferritin → HFE genetic testing → imaging/biopsy if needed
TestFindingNotes
Transferrin saturation↑Most sensitive early marker — best initial test. In UK practice, genotyping is triggered by transferrin saturation >50% (men) or >40% (women) together with a ferritin above the reference range (>300 μg/L men, >200 μg/L women)
Serum ferritin↑↑Confirms iron burden; acute-phase reactant — rises in infection/inflammation, so cannot stand alone
HFE genetic testingC282Y homozygosityConfirms diagnosis when both transferrin sat + ferritin raised
MRI liver/heart (T2*/R2*)↓signal (short T2*)Iron shortens T2*, so loaded tissue loses signal. Non-invasive quantification of liver and cardiac iron — the standard alternative to biopsy
Liver biopsy + Perl’s stainIron deposition, fibrosis stageNo longer needed to diagnose iron overload. Fibrosis assessment (elastography or biopsy) is indicated in confirmed cases with ferritin >1000 μg/L or raised transaminases, to stage fibrosis and exclude cirrhosis (BSH)
LFTs, glucose/HbA1cVariableAssess end-organ damage
USS ± AFP—HCC surveillance once cirrhotic (6-monthly)
Management
Venesection — first-line
  • Weekly venesection until iron depleted
  • Then maintenance venesection typically every 2–4 months, adjusted to keep ferritin at target
  • Targets: transferrin sats <50%, ferritin <50 μg/L
  • Improves fatigue, skin pigmentation and early cardiac dysfunction — but established cirrhosis, arthropathy, hypogonadism and established diabetes do not regress
Iron chelation — second-line
  • Used when venesection contraindicated (e.g. severe anaemia, cardiac instability)
  • Desferrioxamine (subcutaneous)
Lifestyle & complications
  • Avoid alcohol — synergistic liver injury
  • Avoid vitamin C supplements — ↑iron absorption
  • Treat complications: insulin for DM, testosterone for hypogonadism, ACEi/diuretics for cardiomyopathy
  • HCC surveillance (USS ± AFP 6-monthly) if cirrhotic
Genetic counselling
  • Offer HFE genotyping plus transferrin saturation and ferritin to adult first-degree relatives, with counselling. Testing is not offered to healthy children — this is an adult-onset condition
  • Autosomal recessive — siblings at 25% risk of being homozygous, which is not the same as a 25% risk of disease, since penetrance is incomplete
Exam Pearls
C282Y homozygosity (HFE gene, chr 6) = the classic genotype, but penetrance is incomplete — diagnosis needs the genotype plus biochemical iron overload.
Transferrin saturation = best initial test; genotype when it is >50% (men) or >40% (women) with a raised ferritin. Ferritin confirms burden but is an acute-phase reactant — it can’t stand alone.
Presents later in women — menstrual blood loss offsets iron accumulation, so women typically present after the menopause.
Venesection first-line; chelation only when venesection contraindicated. Targets: ferritin <50, transferrin sats <50%.
Venesection improves fatigue, skin pigmentation and early cardiac dysfunction, but established cirrhosis, arthropathy, hypogonadism and diabetes do not regress.
