LIVER__Wilson's Disease:
Overview

Autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene (chromosome 13) -- a copper-transporting protein that normally removes excess copper via bile. Failure leads to progressive copper accumulation in the liver, brain, cornea, and kidneys.

The two organ targets: Liver (hepatitis to cirrhosis) + Brain (basal ganglia to neuro/psychiatric) + Eye (Kayser-Fleischer rings)
Pathophysiology
  • Normally ATP7B moves copper into bile for excretion and loads it onto caeruloplasmin in blood
  • Mutation -- failed biliary copper excretion, and copper is not loaded onto caeruloplasmin. The copper-free protein is unstable and rapidly degraded, so the measured serum level falls (synthesis itself is normal)
  • Copper accumulates: liver first, then brain, cornea, kidneys
  • Caeruloplasmin is LOW despite high total-body copper -- because copper is never loaded onto it, and the copper-free protein is rapidly degraded
Key Facts
  • Autosomal recessive; ATP7B gene, chromosome 13
  • Most present between about 5 and 35 years, but Wilson's has been diagnosed from early childhood into old age
  • Exclude Wilson's in any patient with unexplained liver disease or unexplained neuropsychiatric disease under about 55 — age alone must never be used to exclude it
  • Haemochromatosis is the iron-overload counterpart in the inherited metabolic group
Clinical Features (by site of deposition)
📷 Image placeholder — Kayser-Fleischer ring — a golden-brown to green ring of copper deposited in Descemet's membrane at the corneal periphery, best seen on slit-lamp examination
Liver (usually first)
  • Chronic hepatitis (asymptomatic raised transaminases)
  • Cirrhosis if untreated
  • Acute liver failure -- young + ALF + haemolysis = Wilson's until proven otherwise
Brain -- basal ganglia (later)
  • Parkinsonism: tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity
  • Dysarthria (speech difficulty), dysphagia
  • Dystonia, ataxia
  • Psychiatric: personality change, depression, cognitive impairment, psychosis
Eyes
  • Kayser-Fleischer rings -- copper deposits in Descemet's membrane of the cornea
  • Green-brown rings at the outer rim of the cornea (the limbus), overlying the iris periphery
  • Seen on slit-lamp (not always visible to naked eye)
  • Present in the great majority with neurological Wilson's, but often absent in purely hepatic and presymptomatic disease — their absence never excludes Wilson's. Similar rings occur in chronic cholestatic liver disease, so they are not pathognomonic
Haematological
  • Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia
  • Free copper released from damaged hepatocytes causes oxidative damage to red-cell membranes, producing non-immune haemolysis
  • Negative Coombs = not autoimmune -- distinguishes from autoimmune haemolysis
  • Haemolysis + ALF in a young patient = Wilson's classic presentation
Young patient + acute liver failure + Coombs-negative haemolysis = Wilson's until proven otherwise. Supporting clues on the bloods: a disproportionately low or normal ALP, a low ALP:bilirubin ratio, and an AST:ALT ratio above about 2. Wilsonian ALF is not salvageable with chelation — discuss immediately with a liver transplant centre.
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — MRI brain in Wilson's disease — the "face of the giant panda" sign in the midbrain, with symmetrical high signal in the basal ganglia reflecting copper deposition
Key Tests
  • Serum caeruloplasmin -- first-line screening. Below 0.1 g/L strongly supports Wilson's; 0.1–0.2 g/L is indeterminate
  • Caveat: caeruloplasmin is neither sensitive nor specific -- an acute-phase reactant, so falsely normal or raised with inflammation, infection, cancer, oestrogens or pregnancy; and low in advanced liver failure of any cause, protein loss and some unaffected carriers. Never diagnose or exclude Wilson's on caeruloplasmin alone
  • 24-hour urinary copper HIGH -- >100 mcg/day strongly supports Wilson's in a symptomatic untreated patient, but >40 mcg/day is already abnormal. A value under 100 does not exclude Wilson's, particularly in children and asymptomatic relatives
  • Liver biopsy -- the reference measurement of liver copper (>250 mcg/g dry weight), reserved for diagnostic uncertainty; a normal hepatic copper essentially excludes untreated Wilson's. Often unsafe in coagulopathy and subject to sampling error
  • No single test is confirmatory — diagnosis rests on the combination of caeruloplasmin, urinary copper, KF rings and genetics
Additional Tests
  • Slit-lamp -- Kayser-Fleischer rings
  • MRI brain -- the panda sign (face of the giant panda) with basal ganglia signal change
  • FBC: low Hb, haemolytic picture
  • Coombs test: negative (distinguishes from autoimmune haemolysis)
  • LFTs: raised ALT/AST
  • Genetic testing + screen all first-degree relatives
Management
1
Penicillamine
1st line chelator; increases urinary copper excretion; lifelong. Give pyridoxine alongside (penicillamine is a pyridoxine antagonist). Monitor FBC and urinalysis — frequently at first and after each dose increase — and stop for falling platelets or white cells, or for proteinuria/haematuria. Start low and escalate slowly: chelation can cause paradoxical early neurological worsening
or
2
Trientine
Alternative chelator if penicillamine is not tolerated (rash, nephrotoxicity, bone marrow suppression); generally better tolerated. The same caution about early neurological worsening applies
+
3
Zinc salts
Induce metallothionein in intestinal cells, which traps dietary copper; the copper is then lost as those cells are shed into the gut. Used for maintenance, for presymptomatic patients found on family screening, and in pregnancy
or
4
Liver transplant
Curative -- corrects the hepatic metabolic defect. Indicated for acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis unresponsive to chelation; neurological disease alone is not an indication
Low-copper diet: avoid shellfish, nuts, liver, chocolate. Treatment is lifelong -- do not stop even when well.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Genetics
Autosomal recessive; ATP7B gene, chromosome 13. Copper accumulation due to failed biliary excretion
Classic trigger
Young patient (teens to young adult) + liver disease + neuropsychiatric signs. Onset after 40 is uncommon but well described -- never exclude Wilson's on age alone
Kayser-Fleischer rings
Copper in Descemet's membrane -- green-brown rings at the corneal limbus on slit-lamp. Highly suggestive, especially with neurological signs, but similar rings occur in chronic cholestatic liver disease, so they are not pathognomonic
Basal ganglia = Parkinsonism
Tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, dysarthria, dystonia. Psychiatric features (depression, psychosis) often precede motor signs
Caeruloplasmin caveat
Below 0.1 g/L strongly supports Wilson's; 0.1–0.2 g/L is indeterminate. It is an acute-phase reactant so can be falsely normal, and a low level is also non-specific — it occurs in advanced liver failure of any cause and in some unaffected carriers. Never diagnose or exclude on it alone
24h urine copper
>100 mcg/day strongly supports Wilson's when symptomatic, but >40 mcg/day is already abnormal and a lower value does not exclude it. Liver biopsy copper >250 mcg/g dry weight is the reference measurement, used when non-invasive tests are inconclusive
Coombs-negative haemolysis
Free copper oxidatively damages red-cell membranes, causing non-immune haemolysis. A negative Coombs test distinguishes it from autoimmune haemolysis
Young + ALF + haemolysis
The can't-miss Wilson's presentation. Look for a disproportionately low ALP and an AST:ALT ratio above about 2 — and discuss with a transplant centre immediately, as chelation will not salvage it
Panda sign
MRI brain: the face of the giant panda appearance, with characteristic signal change in the basal ganglia and brainstem
Management
Penicillamine (1st line chelation, with pyridoxine and FBC/urinalysis monitoring) -- trientine if intolerant -- zinc for maintenance and presymptomatic patients. Liver transplant for ALF or decompensated cirrhosis
Screen family
All first-degree relatives — siblings carry a 1-in-4 risk. Targeted ATP7B testing for the proband's known mutation is definitive; caeruloplasmin, 24h urine copper, LFTs and slit-lamp are used alongside it
LIVER__α1-Antitrypsin Deficiency:
Overview

Genetic condition causing low levels of alpha-1 antitrypsin (A1AT) -- a protease inhibitor that normally neutralises neutrophil elastase, protecting elastic tissue. Deficiency causes disease in two organs by two completely opposite mechanisms.

One protein, two organs, opposite mechanisms -- the single most important concept in this topic
OrganMechanismResult
Lungs Loss of function -- too little A1AT in circulation -- unopposed neutrophil elastase destroys alveolar elastin Panacinar emphysema, COPD, bronchiectasis
Liver Gain of toxicity -- mutant A1AT misfolds and is trapped inside hepatocytes -- toxic accumulation causes ER stress and inflammation Hepatitis, fibrosis, cirrhosis, HCC
Lung disease = deficiency (not enough A1AT outside). Liver disease = accumulation (too much mutant A1AT inside hepatocytes). Same protein, opposite problem. The two are largely independent — severe emphysema can occur with a normal liver, and cirrhosis with normal lungs — so assess and monitor both organs separately at diagnosis. Most PiZZ adults never develop clinically significant liver disease.
Genetics
Inheritance
  • Gene: SERPINA1, chromosome 14
  • Inheritance: autosomal co-dominant -- both alleles expressed and contribute; disease severity reflects the combination of both
  • Many variants; M = normal, S and Z = abnormal
Key Pi types (Pi = protease inhibitor; these are phenotypes, written Pi*ZZ as a genotype)
  • PiMM -- normal; full A1AT levels
  • PiMZ -- heterozygote with intermediate levels (inheritance is co-dominant, so "carrier" is loose usage). Little risk alone, but a modifier: it raises fibrosis and cirrhosis risk when there is a second liver insult (alcohol, obesity/type 2 diabetes, viral hepatitis), and lung risk mainly in smokers
  • PiSZ -- moderate deficiency; intermediate risk, mainly lung disease in smokers. PiSS/PiMS -- mild reduction, generally not clinically significant
  • PiZZ -- severe deficiency; highest disease risk; the classic clinical phenotype
  • Z allele: mutant protein misfolds and polymerises in hepatocytes
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — panacinar emphysema on chest CT — widespread destruction of the entire acinus with a basal (lower-zone) predominance, in contrast to the upper-zone centrilobular emphysema of smoking-related COPD
Respiratory (usually presents after 30)
  • Early-onset COPD / emphysema -- especially in a non-smoker or young smoker (emphysema too severe for the smoking history)
  • Panacinar emphysema at the lung bases (contrast: centrilobular at apices in smoking COPD)
  • Bronchiectasis
  • Progressive dyspnoea, wheeze, chronic cough
  • Smoking dramatically accelerates lung destruction
Hepatic
  • Prolonged neonatal cholestasis -- jaundice persisting beyond 14 days with a raised conjugated bilirubin, pale stools and dark urine. Any prolonged neonatal jaundice needs a split bilirubin; a conjugated picture requires urgent referral, as biliary atresia must be excluded
  • Chronic hepatitis, hepatomegaly
  • Cirrhosis at any age
  • Portal hypertension, ascites, varices
  • Increased risk of HCC
Two classic presentations:
1. Young adult with emphysema and minimal or no significant smoking history
2. Child or adult with unexplained cirrhosis, or an infant with prolonged conjugated jaundice
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules on liver biopsy — rounded magenta intracytoplasmic inclusions of misfolded Z-variant A1AT trapped in the hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum; the histological hallmark of A1AT liver disease
Diagnostic
  • Serum A1AT level LOW -- screening test; PiZZ typically <0.5 g/L (check your local laboratory reference range and units, which vary by assay)
  • A1AT is a positive acute-phase protein -- a level taken during infection, an exacerbation or any inflammatory illness may be falsely normal. Interpret alongside CRP, repeat when well, and Pi type anyway if suspicion is high
  • Pi phenotyping (isoelectric focusing) is the usual confirmatory test, with genotyping where the phenotype is ambiguous or a null allele is suspected
Liver Assessment
  • LFTs: raised transaminases if active hepatitis
  • Liver biopsy: PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules in hepatocytes -- the trapped misfolded A1AT; the histological hallmark
  • USS abdomen, fibroscan for cirrhosis staging
Lung Assessment
  • Spirometry: obstructive pattern (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7)
  • HRCT chest: basal emphysema, bronchiectasis
Screening
  • Offer testing (serum A1AT + Pi typing) to first-degree relatives, with genetic counselling
  • Test for A1AT deficiency in COPD or emphysema that is early-onset, disproportionate to the smoking history, in a never-smoker, basal-predominant, or with a positive family history, and in unexplained bronchiectasis, cirrhosis or persistently abnormal LFTs
PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules in hepatocytes are the characteristic (not pathognomonic) histological finding — confirm with A1AT immunohistochemistry, as similar globules occur in other cirrhoses, and they may be absent in early infancy. The diagnosis rests on serum level plus Pi typing; biopsy is for staging or uncertainty
Management
STOP SMOKING -- the single most important intervention; smoking massively amplifies neutrophil elastase activity and accelerates lung destruction
Lung Disease
  • Smoking cessation (most important)
  • Standard COPD management (NICE): treat tobacco dependence, vaccinations, pulmonary rehabilitation, then LAMA + LABA; add an inhaled corticosteroid only where there are asthmatic features or steroid responsiveness, or as a reviewed trial of triple therapy
  • Bronchiectasis care: physiotherapy, airway clearance
  • A1AT augmentation (replacement) therapy -- IV purified A1AT is used in some countries, but is not recommended by NICE and is not routinely available on the NHS; UK management is optimal COPD care plus smoking cessation
  • Lung transplant in end-stage respiratory failure
Liver Disease
  • No disease-modifying drug for hepatic A1AT disease, but risk reduction matters: avoid alcohol, manage weight, type 2 diabetes and metabolic fatty liver, vaccinate against hepatitis A and B, and review hepatotoxic drugs
  • Monitor with LFTs and non-invasive fibrosis assessment; treat cirrhosis complications
  • HCC surveillance: 6-monthly liver ultrasound (± AFP) once cirrhosis is established (NICE) — as for cirrhosis of any cause
  • Liver transplant -- curative for the liver disease: the graft produces normal A1AT, so serum levels normalise and hepatic accumulation stops. It does not reverse emphysema already present, and commits the patient to lifelong immunosuppression
⭐ Exam Pearls
One protein, two mechanisms
Lung = loss of function (deficiency -- no A1AT to inhibit elastase). Liver = gain of toxicity (accumulation -- trapped mutant protein causes ER stress)
SERPINA1, chromosome 14
Autosomal co-dominant. PiZZ = severe. PiSZ = moderate. PiMZ = intermediate levels, a risk modifier rather than benign. PiMM = normal
Classic lung vignette
Young adult with emphysema that's too severe / too early for their smoking history. Think A1AT
Basal emphysema
Panacinar at the lung bases -- distinguishes from smoking COPD (centrilobular emphysema at the apices)
Classic liver presentation
Prolonged conjugated (cholestatic) neonatal jaundice, OR unexplained cirrhosis in a young patient, OR a child with hepatomegaly
HCC risk
A1AT deficiency raises HCC risk, but UK surveillance follows the usual rule: 6-monthly liver ultrasound (± AFP) once cirrhosis is established (NICE). There is no UK recommendation to survey non-cirrhotic patients
Serum A1AT low + genotype
Screening = low serum A1AT. Confirm with Pi genotyping (PiZZ). Don't stop at a low level -- genotype to confirm
PAS-positive globules
Diastase-resistant PAS-positive granules in hepatocytes are characteristic, not pathognomonic — confirm with immunohistochemistry. Diagnosis rests on serum level plus Pi typing
Stop smoking = #1 intervention
Smoking massively amplifies elastase activity. Cessation slows lung decline more than any drug
Liver transplant cures the liver disease
The new liver makes normal A1AT, so serum levels normalise and accumulation stops. Established lung damage is not reversed, so smoking cessation still matters afterwards
A1AT normally inhibits elastase
Remember the normal function: A1AT = the protease inhibitor. Without it, neutrophil elastase runs unchecked in the lung
Smoking + A1AT
Smoking increases neutrophil elastase burden AND inactivates remaining A1AT (oxidation). Double hit -- PiZZ smokers deteriorate very rapidly
LIVER__Primary Biliary Cholangitis:
Overview

Autoimmune destruction of the intrahepatic bile ducts causing chronic cholestasis and, in a minority, progressive fibrosis and cirrhosis. Most patients are not cirrhotic at diagnosis — which is why the disease was renamed from primary biliary cirrhosis to primary biliary cholangitis. A predominantly female disease of middle age.

Instant recognition pattern: middle-aged woman + pruritus + raised ALP + AMA positive = PBC
PBC vs PSC -- the essential contrast
  • PBC: intrahepatic ducts, AMA, middle-aged woman, Sjogren's/RA/sclerosis
  • PSC: intra + extrahepatic ducts, p-ANCA, young man + UC, bile duct beading on MRCP
Autoimmune Associations
  • Sjogren's syndrome
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Systemic sclerosis (CREST)
  • Thyroid disease (Hashimoto's / Graves')
Pathophysiology
1
Autoimmune attack
T-cell mediated destruction of intrahepatic cholangiocytes
to
2
Cholestasis
Progressive bile duct obstruction; bile accumulates
to
3
Fibrosis
Bile back-pressure + inflammation drives periportal fibrosis
to
4
Cirrhosis
Portal hypertension, liver failure
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — xanthelasma — soft yellow cholesterol plaques on the medial upper and lower eyelids, reflecting the hypercholesterolaemia of chronic cholestasis

Typical patient: a woman aged 40–60. Women predominate, but PBC occurs in men and in all ethnic groups — do not discount it on demographics alone.

SymptomsSigns on examination
Pruritus -- often the earliest symptomXanthelasma / xanthomata (cholestasis raises cholesterol)
FatigueExcoriations from scratching
Jaundice (later)Hepatomegaly
Pale, greasy stools and dark urine — late and uncommon, from severe intrahepatic cholestasis (the ducts are normal on imaging)Signs of cirrhosis/portal HTN if advanced (ascites, splenomegaly)
GI symptoms, abdominal discomfortSigns of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (bone pain, bleeding)
Pruritus precedes jaundice -- itch is often the presenting complaint years before the LFTs show bilirubin rise
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — florid duct lesion on liver biopsy — granulomatous destruction of an interlobular bile duct with a dense lymphocytic infiltrate, the histological hallmark of PBC
Key Bloods
  • ALP raised first -- the cholestatic marker; rises early before bilirubin
  • GGT raised (confirms cholestatic pattern)
  • Bilirubin, ALT/AST raised later as disease progresses
  • AMA (anti-mitochondrial antibody) M2 subtype -- the hallmark: present in about 95% of patients and highly specific. About 5–10% of PBC is AMA-negative — a negative AMA with cholestatic LFTs does not exclude PBC. A positive AMA with normal LFTs is not PBC
  • ANA is often positive but generally non-specific. The exceptions are the PBC-specific patterns — anti-sp100 and anti-gp210 — which are highly specific and are used to diagnose AMA-negative PBC
  • IgM raised -- the PBC immunoglobulin (contrast: IgG raised in autoimmune hepatitis)
  • Raised cholesterol (cholestasis)
Imaging and Biopsy
  • USS abdomen -- first-line; excludes biliary obstruction and other pathology
  • MRCP -- normal intrahepatic ducts in PBC (contrast: beading in PSC)
  • Liver biopsy -- not required in a typical case. Cholestatic LFTs plus a positive AMA is enough to diagnose. Biopsy is reserved for AMA-negative disease, suspected overlap with autoimmune hepatitis, or suspected coexisting liver disease; it then shows granulomatous bile duct destruction ("florid duct lesion"). Fibrosis is usually staged non-invasively with transient elastography
IgM (PBC) vs IgG (autoimmune hepatitis) — a useful supporting clue, but not diagnostic on its own. The discrimination rests on the pattern (cholestatic ALP + AMA in PBC vs transaminitis + anti-smooth-muscle/anti-LKM1 + raised IgG in AIH), and overlap syndromes exist
Management
Disease-Modifying
  • Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) -- 1st line for all patients, 13–15 mg/kg/day, lifelong; a non-toxic hydrophilic bile acid that improves liver biochemistry and transplant-free survival. Response is assessed on ALP and bilirubin after 12 months — around a third respond inadequately
  • Second-line (specialist) if there is an inadequate response at 12 months, or UDCA is not tolerated: obeticholic acid, or a PPAR agonist (elafibranor or seladelpar) (NICE). Obeticholic acid is contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis, previous decompensation, or compensated cirrhosis with portal hypertension
Symptomatic / Supportive
  • Colestyramine -- 1st line for pruritus; a bile acid sequestrant that binds bile salts in the gut. Separate the doses from UDCA by at least 2 hours (ideally 4–6), as it also binds UDCA. If ineffective, escalate under specialist advice: rifampicin, then naltrexone, then sertraline
  • Fatigue -- no effective drug therapy, and UDCA does not improve it; screen for and treat reversible contributors (hypothyroidism, anaemia, depression, sleep disturbance)
  • Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) -- check levels and replace if deficient; clinically important mainly in advanced, jaundiced disease
  • Bone protection -- osteoporosis is common. DEXA at diagnosis and periodically; calcium and vitamin D for all; a bisphosphonate if osteoporosis or high fracture risk
  • Monitor and treat portal hypertension complications
Transplant referral: refer to a transplant centre when bilirubin approaches 100 micromol/L, or with decompensation (ascites, encephalopathy, variceal bleeding), or for intractable pruritus. Listing itself is decided on UK end-stage liver disease scoring, not on bilirubin alone
Complications
From Cholestasis
  • Fat malabsorption -- bile deficiency in gut
  • Vitamin D deficiency -- osteomalacia
  • Osteoporosis -- vitamin D deficiency + cholestatic bone disease
  • Xanthelasma / xanthomata -- raised cholesterol
  • Vitamin K deficiency -- bleeding tendency
From Cirrhosis / Portal HTN
  • Ascites
  • Variceal haemorrhage
  • Hepatic encephalopathy
  • HCC -- risk rises once cirrhosis develops, and is higher in men and in UDCA non-responders. Patients with cirrhosis need 6-monthly ultrasound surveillance
⭐ Exam Pearls
Classic patient
Middle-aged woman + pruritus (often first) + raised ALP + AMA-M2 positive = PBC
AMA M2 = hallmark
Highly specific for PBC and positive in about 95% of patients. But 5–10% of PBC is AMA-negative, diagnosed on PBC-specific ANA (anti-sp100/anti-gp210) or biopsy
IgM raised (not IgG)
PBC tends to raise IgM, autoimmune hepatitis IgG. A supporting clue, not diagnostic on its own, and overlap syndromes exist in the autoimmune liver group
ALP first
ALP rises before bilirubin in PBC -- it's a cholestatic disease, not initially hepatitic
Pruritus before jaundice
Itch is often the first symptom, years before bilirubin rises. Itch + raised ALP in a middle-aged woman = think PBC
PBC vs PSC
PBC = intrahepatic ducts, AMA, woman, Sjogren's/RA. PSC = intra+extrahepatic, p-ANCA, man + UC, MRCP beading
1st line = UDCA
Ursodeoxycholic acid 13–15 mg/kg/day, lifelong. Check ALP and bilirubin at 12 months — an inadequate response means second-line therapy (obeticholic acid, or elafibranor/seladelpar)
Pruritus Rx = colestyramine
Separate doses from UDCA by at least 2 hours (ideally 4–6). Rifampicin, then naltrexone, then sertraline if it fails. A bile acid sequestrant -- binds bile salts in the gut, reducing systemic levels
ADEK
Cholestasis impairs fat absorption — check fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K and replace if deficient, mainly in advanced jaundiced disease. Vitamin D and calcium routinely for bone protection
Transplant referral
Refer when bilirubin approaches 100 micromol/L, or with decompensation or intractable pruritus; listing itself is decided on UK end-stage liver disease scoring. This is the major referral trigger in PBC
Xanthelasma mechanism
Cholestasis -- raised serum cholesterol -- lipid deposits around eyes and tendons
Autoimmune associations
Sjogren's, RA, systemic sclerosis, thyroid disease -- PBC rarely occurs in isolation
LIVER__Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis:
Overview

Chronic cholestatic disease characterised by progressive fibrosis and stricturing of both the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, leading to cirrhosis. Strongly associated with ulcerative colitis.

Instant recognition pattern: a man in his 30s or 40s + colitis + raised ALP = PSC
PSC vs PBC -- the essential contrast
  • PSC: intra + extrahepatic ducts, p-ANCA, man aged 30-40, UC association
  • PBC: intrahepatic ducts only, AMA, middle-aged woman, Sjogren's/RA/sclerosis
  • PSC: no disease-modifying drug. PBC: UDCA slows progression
Risk Factors
  • Male sex (2:1 male predominance)
  • Age 30-40 years
  • Inflammatory bowel disease -- about 70% of PSC patients have IBD, most commonly ulcerative colitis, but around one in eight has Crohn's colitis
  • Positive family history
About 70% of PSC patients have IBD -- every patient needs ileocolonoscopy with biopsies at diagnosis, even if asymptomatic. PSC may precede IBD, follow it by years, or occur without it, and the colitis is typically mild or quiescent, extensive with a right-sided predominance, often with rectal sparing and backwash ileitis
Clinical Features
Symptoms
  • Pruritus (often early)
  • Fatigue
  • RUQ pain
  • Jaundice (cholestatic -- pale stools, dark urine)
  • Fever/rigors if bacterial cholangitis supervenes
Signs
  • Hepatosplenomegaly
  • Jaundice, excoriations
  • Signs of cirrhosis if advanced
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — MRCP in PSC — multifocal strictures alternating with dilatations of the intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts producing the classic "beaded" / string-of-beads appearance
Bloods
  • ALP raised (cholestatic pattern) -- the dominant LFT abnormality
  • Bilirubin raised (later in disease)
  • GGT raised
  • p-ANCA is often positive but is not diagnostic -- it also occurs in autoimmune hepatitis and in ulcerative colitis without liver disease, and a negative result does not exclude PSC. Unlike AMA in PBC, there is no diagnostic autoantibody in PSC
  • Serum IgG4 -- check at diagnosis; IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis is the key mimic, looks the same on MRCP, and responds to corticosteroids
  • PT/INR, albumin (synthetic function)
Imaging and Endoscopy
  • MRCP -- the diagnostic investigation of choice; shows bile duct strictures with the classic "beaded" / string-of-beads appearance (alternating strictures and dilatations). The diagnosis requires typical cholangiographic findings with secondary causes excluded (IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis, previous biliary surgery, ischaemia, HIV cholangiopathy). ERCP is no longer used to make the diagnosis -- it is reserved for treating a symptomatic dominant stricture and taking brushings, because of its pancreatitis and cholangitis risk
  • USS abdomen -- first-line; may show dilated ducts
  • Ileocolonoscopy with biopsies -- mandatory at diagnosis to assess for colitis, even if the patient has no bowel symptoms
  • Liver biopsy -- if diagnostic uncertainty; shows periductal "onion-skin" fibrosis
MRCP: beaded bile ducts = PSC. Normal intrahepatic ducts on MRCP = PBC (no beading)
Management
No proven disease-modifying drug for PSC -- unlike PBC (UDCA), there is no equivalent therapy that slows progression. UDCA is not recommended in PSC: it improves ALP but not survival, and high-dose UDCA is harmful
Stricture Management
  • ERCP for a symptomatic dominant stricture (jaundice, pruritus or cholangitis) -- balloon dilatation, with brushings and biopsy mandatory to exclude cholangiocarcinoma. Stenting is reserved for when dilatation alone is insufficient
  • Antibiotic cover with ERCP (reduces risk of bacterial cholangitis)
  • Treat acute cholangitis: IV antibiotics (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam)
Symptomatic / Supportive
  • Colestyramine -- first-line for pruritus (a bile acid sequestrant)
  • Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) -- supplement; cholestasis impairs absorption
  • Bone protection -- DEXA at diagnosis and periodically; bisphosphonate if osteoporosis or high fracture risk
  • Monitor and manage portal hypertension
Surveillance
  • Annual abdominal ultrasound -- chiefly to detect gallbladder polyps and gallbladder cancer. Routine CA19-9 is not recommended for cholangiocarcinoma surveillance: it is neither sensitive nor specific and rises in cholangitis. New jaundice, weight loss or rapid biochemical deterioration should prompt urgent MRI/MRCP
  • Annual colonoscopic surveillance from the time of PSC diagnosis in anyone with PSC and colitis -- colorectal cancer risk is several-fold higher than in colitis alone. Those with PSC and no colitis need much less frequent colonoscopy
  • Regular OGD (varices if cirrhotic)
  • Liver transplant -- the only definitive treatment and the only one that alters long-term survival, but not curative: PSC recurs in the graft in a minority. Beyond decompensated cirrhosis, PSC-specific indications include intractable pruritus and recurrent bacterial cholangitis
Complications
📷 Image placeholder — periductal "onion-skin" fibrosis on liver biopsy — concentric rings of fibrous tissue encircling an interlobular bile duct, the histological hallmark of PSC
Malignancy
  • Cholangiocarcinoma -- PSC is the single strongest risk factor; risk is lifelong and highest soon after PSC is diagnosed. Any new jaundice, weight loss or sudden rise in bilirubin needs urgent imaging
  • Gallbladder cancer -- gallbladder polyps are common in PSC and carry a high risk of malignancy, so a polyp of any size warrants cholecystectomy; this is what the annual ultrasound looks for
  • Colorectal cancer -- in those with concurrent colitis; annual colonoscopy from the time of PSC diagnosis
  • HCC (if cirrhotic)
Other Complications
  • Recurrent bacterial cholangitis (from bile stasis + strictures)
  • Cirrhosis and portal hypertension (ascites, varices)
  • Fat malabsorption + fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
  • Osteoporosis (vitamin D deficiency + cholestatic bone disease)
Two cancers to fear in PSC: cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct) + colorectal cancer (if UC). Both require active surveillance.

Man aged 30-40 + ulcerative colitis + raised ALP = PSC until proven otherwise

Mostly UC, but around one in eight is Crohn's colitis. Always scope with biopsies at diagnosis. Conversely, only a small minority of UC patients develop PSC
MRCP = investigation of choice
Beaded / string-of-beads appearance of the bile ducts. ERCP is now therapeutic and for tissue sampling only
p-ANCA is not diagnostic
Often positive, but also seen in autoimmune hepatitis and in UC without liver disease; a negative result does not exclude PSC. Unlike AMA in PBC, there is no diagnostic autoantibody

Ducts (both vs intrahepatic), antibody (p-ANCA vs AMA), sex (male vs female), IBD (UC vs none), drug (no UDCA vs UDCA works)

Unlike PBC (UDCA slows progression), PSC has no proven equivalent. Management = strictures + surveillance + transplant

PSC is the #1 risk factor; risk is highest soon after diagnosis. Annual ultrasound is for gallbladder polyps -- routine CA19-9 is not recommended. New jaundice or weight loss needs urgent imaging

The only definitive treatment, but not curative -- PSC recurs in the graft in a minority. Also indicated for intractable pruritus and recurrent bacterial cholangitis
LIVER__Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease:
Overview — The Disease Spectrum
NAFLD = excess fat in hepatocytes without significant alcohol use. The commonest cause of liver disease in the developed world. Essentially the liver manifestation of metabolic syndrome. NASH is histologically very similar to, and often indistinguishable from, alcoholic hepatitis — the distinction is made on the alcohol history, not the biopsy.
Nomenclature: NAFLD has been renamed MASLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease) and NASH renamed MASH; simple steatosis, formerly NAFL, is MASL. MASLD is a positive diagnosis — hepatic steatosis plus at least one cardiometabolic risk factor (overweight/obesity, type 2 diabetes or dysglycaemia, hypertension, raised triglycerides, low HDL) — rather than a diagnosis of exclusion. UK guidance (NICE) now uses MASLD/MASH. NAFLD and NASH remain in wide use for the same disease, so recognise both.

Simple fat accumulation. Often reversible with lifestyle change.
→
2

→

Irreversible. Portal hypertension, liver failure, hepatocellular carcinoma risk — once cirrhosis is present, offer 6-monthly ultrasound surveillance for HCC (NICE).
Risk Factors — Metabolic Syndrome
Main risk factors
  • Obesity (BMI >30) — the strongest driver
  • Type 2 diabetes — insulin resistance promotes hepatic lipid accumulation
  • Hyperlipidaemia (particularly hypertriglyceridaemia)
  • Hypertension
  • Together = metabolic syndrome
Other causes (secondary steatosis, not MASLD itself)
  • Rapid weight loss / starvation — fatty acid mobilisation outpaces export
  • Certain drugs (amiodarone, methotrexate, tamoxifen, steroids)
  • Total parenteral nutrition (prolonged)
Key clinical trigger: T2DM + deranged LFTs → think NAFLD first.
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — macrovesicular steatosis on liver histology — hepatocytes distended by large fat droplets that displace the nucleus; in NASH there is additional ballooning degeneration, Mallory-Denk bodies and lobular inflammation (identical to alcoholic hepatitis)
Usually asymptomatic — most cases found incidentally on routine bloods or USS requested for another reason. Features when present: fatigue, vague RUQ discomfort, hepatomegaly. Advanced disease presents with features of cirrhosis (ascites, jaundice, varices — see Liver Cirrhosis note).
Investigations — The Staged Fibrosis Pathway
📷 Image placeholder — hepatic steatosis on ultrasound — a diffusely bright (hyperechoic) liver, brighter than the renal cortex, with loss of definition of the portal vein walls and diaphragm
Bloods
  • ALT > AST — typical of early MASLD, whereas AST:ALT ≥2:1 suggests alcohol-related disease. The ratio rises above 1 as fibrosis advances, so neither pattern is decisive
  • Liver blood tests are often normal — including in people who already have advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis. Normal LFTs do not rule out MASLD and must not be used to assess fibrosis; an incidentally fatty liver on ultrasound is suspected MASLD even with normal LFTs (NICE)
  • ↑GGT, ↑ALP (milder than alcoholic)
  • Fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid profile (identify metabolic drivers)
  • FBC, clotting, albumin (synthetic function if advanced)
  • Exclude other causes: viral hepatitis serology, autoimmune markers, ferritin (haemochromatosis)
Imaging
  • Liver USS — first-line; steatosis = ↑ echogenicity ("bright liver")
  • FibroScan (transient elastography) — quantifies liver stiffness → estimates fibrosis stage non-invasively
  • Liver biopsy — the reference standard; stages fibrosis (F0–F4) and excludes other pathology; reserved for when non-invasive tests are equivocal
NICE-recommended fibrosis assessment pathway:

→

If ELF unavailable: use FIB-4 score or NAFLD Fibrosis Score + FibroScan as alternatives.
Management
Lifestyle modification is the cornerstone of treatment — the intervention that most reliably reduces steatosis and slows progression. Drug treatments for MASH with fibrosis are now licensed in the UK but are specialist-initiated and not yet routinely available on the NHS pending NICE appraisal.
Lifestyle — first-line for all patients
  • Weight loss — the most effective intervention, and the benefit is graded: around 5% reduces liver fat, around 7% is associated with resolution of steatohepatitis, and 10% or more with improvement in fibrosis
  • Low-calorie diet (Mediterranean diet preferred — high in olive oil, fish, fibre)
  • Regular aerobic exercise (reduces hepatic fat independently of weight loss)
  • Alcohol — advise staying within the UK low-risk limits (no more than 14 units a week, spread over 3 or more days); advise abstinence if there is advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis
  • Control metabolic risk factors: treat T2DM, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia
Specialist options (for NASH / advanced fibrosis)
  • Vitamin E — antioxidant; considered in secondary care for adults with advanced liver fibrosis, whether or not they have diabetes (off-label) (NICE)
  • Pioglitazone (thiazolidinedione) — improves insulin sensitivity; considered in secondary care for adults with advanced liver fibrosis, whether or not they have diabetes (off-label; avoid in heart failure and in past or active bladder cancer) (NICE)
  • GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide) — now licensed in the UK for adults with MASH and moderate-to-advanced fibrosis; substantial weight loss with histological improvement. Specialist-initiated
  • Resmetirom — a thyroid hormone receptor-β agonist, licensed in the UK for MASH with moderate-to-advanced fibrosis. Specialist-initiated
  • Bariatric surgery — produces the largest sustained weight loss and can improve or resolve steatohepatitis; offered on the usual obesity criteria, not for liver disease alone
  • Liver transplantation — for decompensated cirrhosis (NAFLD now a leading indication)

Typical of early disease; AST:ALT ≥2:1 suggests alcohol. The ratio rises as fibrosis advances, and LFTs may be normal throughout — neither pattern is decisive.

Insulin resistance drives hepatic lipid accumulation. But normal LFTs do not rule it out — they are often normal even with advanced fibrosis.

First-line imaging. Confirms steatosis but cannot stage fibrosis.

LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acute Liver Fai:
Overview

Acute hepatitis = acute inflammation/injury of the liver — often self-limiting and recoverable. Acute liver failure (ALF) = the catastrophic endpoint where the liver fails outright.

ALF diagnostic triad: Jaundice + Coagulopathy (INR >1.5) + Hepatic encephalopathy — in a patient with no pre-existing liver disease
ALF vs Acute-on-Chronic
  • ALF — triad in a previously healthy liver; potentially reversible
  • Acute-on-chronic LF — same triad but on background of known liver disease (cirrhosis)
  • No chronic stigmata in true ALF (no splenomegaly, spider naevi, ascites) — the liver was healthy until days ago
ALF vs Cirrhosis
  • ALF: no prior liver disease, acute onset, potentially reversible
  • Cirrhosis: chronic, irreversible fibrosis with portal hypertension
  • Encephalopathy + coagulopathy in a previously healthy liver = ALF until proven otherwise
Classification (by jaundice to encephalopathy interval)

The interval from jaundice onset to encephalopathy development is prognostically important.

TypeIntervalKey note
Hyperacute<7 daysOften paracetamol; paradoxically better spontaneous survival
Acute1-4 weeksIntermediate prognosis
Subacute4-12 weeksOften worse prognosis; harder to diagnose
Aetiology
Paracetamol overdose = commonest UK cause of ALF
📷 Image placeholder — paracetamol treatment nomogram — plasma paracetamol concentration against time since ingestion; a single UK treatment line runs from 100 mg/L at 4 h to ~15 mg/L at 15 h. Any level on or above the line → treat with N-acetylcysteine
Main Causes
  • Paracetamol overdose -- #1 UK cause; dose-dependent hepatotoxicity via NAPQI
  • Viral hepatitis -- A, B, E (and B+D co-infection)
  • Drugs/toxins -- non-paracetamol DILI: idiosyncratic drug reactions, herbal supplements, Amanita phalloides (death cap mushroom)
  • Vascular -- Budd-Chiari syndrome, ischaemic hepatitis ("shock liver")
  • Pregnancy-related -- acute fatty liver of pregnancy, HELLP syndrome
  • Metabolic -- Wilson's disease (especially young patients)
  • Autoimmune hepatitis
  • Seronegative -- no cause found (poor prognosis)
Risk Factors for Paracetamol Toxicity
  • Chronic alcohol misuse
  • Fasting / poor nutrition (depletes glutathione)
  • Concurrent enzyme-inducing drugs (antiepileptics, rifampicin)
These affect susceptibility, not the treatment decision: since the single UK treatment line was introduced, every patient with a known ingestion time is assessed against the same line, whatever their risk factors (MHRA).
Young patient + ALF + haemolytic anaemia -- think Wilson's disease (Kayser-Fleischer rings, low caeruloplasmin)
Hepatitis E -- now the commonest acute viral hepatitis in the UK (zoonotic genotype 3); the genotype 1 infection seen in endemic areas carries a high mortality in pregnancy

  • Coagulopathy (bruising, bleeding)
  • Cerebral oedema -- raised ICP (headache, papilloedema, Cushing's triad)

  • Sepsis / infection (immune dysfunction)
Cerebral oedema with raised ICP is a leading cause of death in ALF

Distinguishing ALF from decompensated cirrhosis: In ALF there are no chronic stigmata -- absent splenomegaly, spider angiomata, palmar erythema, and caput medusae. The liver was previously healthy.

LIVER__Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC):
Definition & The Core Concept
📷 Image placeholder — gross pathology of hepatocellular carcinoma — a large tumour nodule arising within a coarsely nodular, cirrhotic liver, often with areas of necrosis and haemorrhage

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) = a primary malignancy of hepatocytes and the commonest primary liver cancer. It is a leading cause of cancer death worldwide.

The core concept: HCC almost always arises on a background of chronic liver disease / cirrhosis (~80–90% of cases). Think of it as the end-stage complication of long-standing liver injury — which is why surveillance of at-risk patients is central.
Key exception: chronic hepatitis B can cause HCC without cirrhosis (the virus is directly oncogenic and integrates into the host genome).
Risk Factors

Cirrhosis of ANY cause is the dominant risk factor. The common drivers are:

🦠 Viral hepatitis
  • Chronic hepatitis B — commonest cause worldwide (can cause HCC without cirrhosis)
  • Chronic hepatitis C — historically a major cause in the West, now declining with direct-acting antiviral treatment (via cirrhosis)
🍺 Metabolic / toxic
  • Alcohol-related liver disease — together with MASLD, the leading underlying cause of HCC in the UK
  • MASLD / MASH (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease; formerly NAFLD/NASH) — a rapidly rising cause with obesity and diabetes
  • Diabetes, obesity, smoking, anabolic steroids
🧬 Inherited liver disease
  • Haemochromatosis (high risk)
  • α1-antitrypsin deficiency
  • Autoimmune hepatitis, PBC (via cirrhosis)
🌾 Aflatoxin
  • Toxin from Aspergillus flavus on poorly-stored grain/nuts
  • Synergistic with hepatitis B; causes a characteristic TP53 mutation
Surveillance & Screening
6-monthly liver ultrasound (± alpha-fetoprotein) is offered to adults with cirrhosis, and to selected patients with chronic hepatitis B (those with significant fibrosis or cirrhosis) — in hepatitis B, AFP is measured as well as the ultrasound. It is not offered to people who would not be fit for any HCC treatment — for example decompensated cirrhosis who would not be transplant candidates, very poor performance status, or those receiving end-of-life care. Surveillance detects tumours early, when curative treatment is still possible. A new or enlarging focal lesion on a surveillance scan needs urgent referral to the HCC MDT with multiphase contrast CT or MRI — not a repeat scan at the next 6-month slot.
Why it matters
  • HCC is usually asymptomatic until advanced
  • Curative options (resection, transplant, ablation) depend on small, early tumours
Clinical Features
🚩 Red flag — decompensation
  • Unexpected decompensation of previously stable cirrhosis: new ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy or variceal bleed → think HCC
🩺 Symptoms & signs
  • Often asymptomatic early
  • RUQ pain, hepatomegaly / a hard mass, weight loss, anorexia, malaise
  • In primary care, consider an urgent direct-access ultrasound within 2 weeks in anyone with an upper abdominal mass consistent with an enlarged liver (NICE)
  • Signs of chronic liver disease; a liver bruit may be heard
🧪 Paraneoplastic
  • Hypoglycaemia
  • Polycythaemia / erythrocytosis (ectopic EPO)
  • Hypercalcaemia (PTHrP)
⚠️ Complications
  • Vascular invasion → portal vein thrombosis / Budd-Chiari
  • Spontaneous tumour rupture → haemoperitoneum
  • Metastases (lung, bone, nodes)
Investigations & Diagnosis
📷 Image placeholder — multiphase contrast CT of HCC — a liver lesion showing avid arterial-phase enhancement ("wash-in") followed by contrast "wash-out" on the portal-venous/delayed phase; in a cirrhotic liver this pattern is diagnostic without biopsy
🩸 Bloods
  • Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) — tumour marker; often raised but can be normal, so it does not exclude HCC (used for surveillance/monitoring, not diagnosis alone)
  • LFTs, clotting, FBC; hepatitis serology; assess synthetic function
🖥️ Imaging — the diagnosis
  • Ultrasound (surveillance / initial)
  • Multiphase contrast CT or MRI: HCC shows arterial-phase enhancement (“wash-in”) with venous/delayed-phase “wash-out”
  • In a cirrhotic liver this appearance is often diagnostic without biopsy
Biopsy is usually avoided when imaging is diagnostic — principally because the imaging appearance is itself diagnostic, so biopsy adds nothing; it also carries a small risk of bleeding and of tumour seeding along the needle track. It is reserved for uncertain cases.
🎯 Staging & work-up
  • CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for metastases and vascular invasion
  • Assess liver function (Child-Pugh) and performance status — these determine treatment eligibility as much as the tumour itself
Management

Decisions are guided by the BCLC (Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer) staging system, which combines tumour burden + liver function + performance status. Managed by a specialist MDT.

IntentOptions
Curative (early, preserved liver function)Surgical resection (single tumour, good function, no significant portal hypertension); liver transplantation (treats tumour + cirrhosis); ablation (radiofrequency/microwave) for small tumours
IntermediateTACE (transarterial chemoembolisation)
AdvancedSystemic therapy: atezolizumab + bevacizumab is first-line (preserved liver function, good performance status); a tyrosine-kinase inhibitor (lenvatinib or sorafenib) if immunotherapy is unsuitable
Terminal (poor liver function / performance status)Best supportive & palliative care
Milan criteria (for transplant): a single tumour ≤5 cm, or up to 3 nodules each ≤3 cm, with no vascular invasion or metastases — transplantation removes both the cancer and the diseased liver.
Prognosis is generally poor (late presentation on a background of cirrhosis) and depends on tumour stage and residual liver function. Prevention — hepatitis B vaccination, antiviral treatment of chronic hepatitis, alcohol reduction and cirrhosis surveillance — is the highest-impact intervention.
Exam Pearls
The big risk factor
Cirrhosis of any cause. Chronic hepatitis B can cause HCC even WITHOUT cirrhosis (directly oncogenic).
Classic vignette
Sudden decompensation of previously stable cirrhosis — new ascites/jaundice → think HCC.
Tumour marker
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) — useful but can be normal, so a normal AFP does not exclude HCC.
Diagnosis
Often radiological in a cirrhotic liver: arterial-phase wash-in, venous/delayed wash-out on CT/MRI — biopsy usually avoided, since the imaging is itself diagnostic.
Surveillance
6-monthly ultrasound (± AFP) in cirrhosis, and in selected hepatitis B patients (ultrasound and AFP). Not offered to those who would not be fit for HCC treatment.
Transplant
Milan criteria: single ≤5 cm or up to 3 nodules ≤3 cm, no vascular invasion/mets.
Aflatoxin
Aspergillus flavus toxin, synergistic with hepatitis B; causes a TP53 mutation.
Advanced therapy
Atezolizumab + bevacizumab is first-line; a TKI (lenvatinib/sorafenib) if immunotherapy is unsuitable.
